Q011405:
## Looking at one continuous feature
Before choosing a transformation or an algorithm, a practitioner looks at the distribution of each feature: is it symmetric, skewed, multimodal, or does it contain extreme values? The distribution of a single continuous variable is shown by a histogram, which splits the value range into bins and shows how many rows fall in each. This is a generally accepted exploratory-analysis practice.
## In Databricks
Notebook and SQL editor visualizations include a histogram type. The Databricks documentation describes it as plotting how frequently a value occurs, showing whether values cluster around a few ranges or are spread out, as a bar chart in which you control the number of bins. Histogram charts also support backend aggregation, so queries over more than 64,000 rows are not truncated.
- A long right tail and several peaks are both visible at a glance; changing the bin count shows more or less detail.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Histogram (correct):** it shows how often values fall into each range, so skew (a long tail on one side) and clusters (several peaks) are visible directly, and the bin count can be tuned.
- ✗ **B. Counter display:** a counter shows one aggregate number such as the mean. A single average cannot reveal skew or clusters, which is exactly what the question asks about.
- ✗ **C. Word cloud:** a word cloud sizes words by frequency and is meant for text. Numbers as words give no sense of value ranges or ordering.
- ✗ **D. Pie chart:** a pie chart shows the proportion of a whole across a few categories; ten arbitrary slices hide the shape of a continuous distribution and are hard to compare by eye.

## Key idea
To see the shape of one continuous feature, use a histogram (bins show skew and clusters), not a pie, counter or word cloud.
Q011406:
## Continuous values grouped by a category
When one feature is numeric and the other categorical, the useful question is how the numeric distribution differs between groups. A box plot summarizes each group with its median, quartiles (the interquartile range) and whiskers or outlying points, so groups can be compared side by side. This is a generally accepted exploratory-analysis technique.
## In Databricks
The box chart visualization in notebooks and the SQL editor shows the distribution summary of numerical data, optionally grouped by a category. The documentation says it lets you compare value ranges across categories and see the location, spread and skewness of groups through their quartiles. The docs also note that box charts aggregate only up to 64,000 rows; larger datasets are truncated, so sample or aggregate first.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Pie chart:** a pie shows proportions of a whole across a few categories; one slice per fare value is unreadable and carries no quartile information.
- ✗ **B. Line chart by row number:** row order is arbitrary here, so the line shows no per-category summary and mixes all payment types together.
- ✗ **C. Scatter chart:** a scatter chart shows the relationship between two numeric variables. Putting a categorical column on both axes produces only a grid of identical points and says nothing about the spread of fares.
- ✓ **D. Box chart (correct):** it draws one box per category with median, interquartile range and outlying values, which is the per-group spread comparison the analyst asked for.

## Key idea
Numeric spread per category is a box chart (median, quartiles, outliers per group); histograms show one distribution, scatter charts show two numeric variables.
Q011407:
## Frequencies of a categorical feature
A categorical feature has no meaningful numeric distribution, so the usual check is a count per category. A bar chart with one bar per category shows class balance (for example, 90% / 8% / 2%), which matters because imbalanced labels change how a model is trained and evaluated. This is a generally accepted exploratory-analysis practice.
## In Databricks
For bar, line, area, pie and heatmap charts the visualization editor can aggregate the Y-axis column itself (for example a count), so you do not rewrite the query to add an aggregation column. The documentation points out that this aggregation applies to the entire dataset, not just the first 64,000 rows shown in a table. Bar charts also support backend aggregation, so queries returning more than 64K rows are not truncated.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Scatter chart:** a scatter chart plots two numeric variables. Fifty million points for a three-valued category would overlap into three lines and show no counts.
- ✗ **B. Box chart:** a box chart summarizes a numeric value per category; the label has no numeric value to summarize and the chart would not display class counts.
- ✓ **C. Bar chart with visualization aggregation (correct):** counting rows per category in the chart settings shows the class proportions over the full dataset without editing the underlying query.
- ✗ **D. Histogram with many narrow bins:** a histogram bins a numeric range. A categorical label has no range, so most bins would be empty.

## Key idea
Class balance of a categorical feature is a bar chart of counts per category; let the visualization aggregate over the whole dataset.
Q011408:
## Display rows versus the full dataset
A notebook result table shows a limited number of rows. If a visualization is built on those displayed rows with no aggregation, the chart reflects only that subset, and a statistic computed from it can differ from the same statistic over all rows. This is why a plotted average can disagree with a Spark aggregation.
## The Databricks fix
The documentation says that for bar, line, area, pie and heatmap charts you can turn on aggregation in the visualization itself, and that the aggregation applies to the entire dataset rather than the first 64,000 rows displayed in a table. Alternatively aggregate in the query first and plot the small result.
- A summary computed in Spark (`groupBy`) always uses all rows; the chart on a truncated table does not.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Region name length:** `avg` groups by the whole value of `region`, whatever its length; this is not how grouping works.
- ✓ **B. First 64,000 rows (correct):** the chart used only the displayed subset, so its averages are estimates from that subset. Turn on the chart's aggregation or aggregate in the query to use all 12 million rows.
- ✗ **C. Rounding:** bar charts do not round values to integers; the small differences are not whole-number rounding.
- ✗ **D. Stale cache:** a cleared cache would cause a recompute, not different averages, and the chart is built from the cell's own result, not from a previous cluster.

## Key idea
A chart on a displayed table covers only the first 64,000 rows; enable the visualization aggregation (whole dataset) or aggregate in the query.
Q011409:
## What a distribution view must show
The distribution of a continuous feature is its spread: center, range, skew and outliers. Two standard exploratory charts do this for one variable: the histogram (frequency per bin) and the box plot (median, quartiles, outlying values). This is a generally accepted exploratory-analysis definition.
## Databricks chart types
Notebook and SQL editor visualizations include histogram and box charts. Pie charts show proportions of categories, counter displays show a single number, and word clouds show text frequency.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Word cloud:** sizes words by frequency; it is a text visual, not a numeric distribution.
- ✗ **B. Pie chart:** shows shares of categories, not a continuous spread.
- ✓ **C. Histogram (correct):** bins of the value range show shape, skew and clusters of one feature.
- ✗ **D. Counter display:** gives one headline number such as an average and no information about shape or spread.
- ✓ **E. Box chart (correct):** shows median, interquartile range and outlying points of one numeric feature, and can be grouped by a category if needed.

## Key idea
Histogram and box chart are the single-variable distribution views for a continuous feature.
Q011410:
## Two continuous features
For two numeric features the standard question is how strongly one changes with the other. The Pearson correlation coefficient measures the strength and direction of a linear relationship on a scale from -1 to 1; Spearman correlation does the same for rank (monotonic) relationships. These are generally accepted statistical definitions.
## In Spark ML
`pyspark.ml.stat.Correlation` computes a correlation matrix over a vector column and supports the methods Pearson (default) and Spearman. The chi-squared test, by contrast, requires categorical features and labels.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Comparing modes:** modes describe the most frequent value of each column separately and say nothing about how the two columns vary together.
- ✗ **B. Chi-squared test:** Spark's `ChiSquareTest` converts feature/label pairs into a contingency matrix and requires categorical values, so raw continuous columns do not fit.
- ✗ **C. Distinct counts:** cardinality describes each column separately and is unrelated to joint movement.
- ✓ **D. Pearson correlation (correct):** it gives a single number between -1 and 1 describing the linear association of the two continuous columns, and Spark ML computes it with `Correlation.corr`.

## Key idea
Two continuous features are compared with correlation (Pearson for linear, Spearman for monotonic); chi-squared needs categorical data.
Q011411:
## Association between categorical variables
For two categorical variables the standard test is Pearson's chi-squared test of independence. It builds a contingency table of observed counts, compares it with the counts expected if the variables were independent, and returns a statistic and p-value. This is a generally accepted statistical definition.
## In Spark ML
The Spark documentation states that `spark.ml` supports Pearson's chi-squared tests for independence. `ChiSquareTest` runs the test for every feature against the label; the (feature, label) pairs are converted into a contingency matrix, and all label and feature values must be categorical.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. OneHotEncoder:** it transforms categories into vectors for modeling. It is a preprocessing step and gives no p-value.
- ✓ **B. ChiSquareTest (correct):** it tests independence of each categorical feature against a categorical label and returns p-values, matching the question.
- ✗ **C. Imputer with mode:** Imputer fills missing values; it does not test any relationship (and Spark documents that it does not support categorical features).
- ✗ **D. Spearman correlation:** it ranks numeric values; arbitrary category indices have no meaningful order, so a rank correlation of them is not an independence test.

## Key idea
Categorical-vs-categorical independence is a chi-squared test (`ChiSquareTest` in Spark ML), which needs categorical inputs.
Q011412:
## Choosing the comparison by feature types
The right statistic depends on the types of the two features.
- Continuous vs continuous: correlation (Pearson or Spearman).
- Categorical vs categorical: chi-squared test of independence.
- Continuous vs a two-level categorical: compare the group means with a two-sample t-test (or a rank-based test when the data are not normal); with more than two groups, an ANOVA. These are generally accepted statistical definitions.
## On Databricks
Spark ML ships correlation and chi-squared tests in `pyspark.ml.stat`; group-mean tests such as the t-test are usually done on a sample with `scipy.stats` (single node) or by comparing group aggregates and a box chart.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Two-sample t-test (correct):** it tests whether the means of a continuous variable differ between two groups, which is exactly a continuous feature split by a two-level categorical feature.
- ✗ **B. Correlation of a column with itself:** this is trivially 1 and tells nothing about group differences.
- ✗ **C. Bar chart of distinct values:** that is a frequency view of one column and does not compare group means.
- ✗ **D. Chi-squared:** Spark's version needs categorical values; a continuous variable would have to be binned first, losing information.

## Key idea
Match the test to the types: numeric-numeric is correlation, category-category is chi-squared, numeric by two groups is a t-test.
Q011413:
## What a correlation coefficient measures
Pearson's coefficient measures the strength of a linear relationship. A symmetric curve such as a U or parabola has positive slope on one side and negative on the other, so the linear effects cancel and the coefficient is near zero even though `y` is a deterministic function of `x`. A coefficient near zero therefore means "no linear association", not "no association". This is a generally accepted statistical fact.
- Always plot the two features (scatter chart) before trusting a single number.
- Spearman measures monotonic association and would also miss a U shape; a transformation (such as squaring) or a nonlinear model can capture it.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Chart error:** the chart is right; opposing slopes cancel and produce a near-zero coefficient.
- ✗ **B. Zero means independent:** zero correlation does not imply independence; here `y` depends on `x` completely.
- ✗ **C. Replace with the mean:** Pearson is valid for linear relationships; the mean is a one-column summary and says nothing about two variables together.
- ✓ **D. Strong but nonlinear (correct):** the two sides of the U cancel in a linear measure, so the near-zero Pearson value is consistent with a clear dependence, which the scatter chart reveals.

## Key idea
Correlation near zero means no linear relationship only; check a scatter chart for nonlinear patterns.
Q011414:
## Collinear features
When two predictors are almost perfectly correlated (multicollinearity), they carry nearly the same information. A linear model cannot separate their effects, so coefficients become unstable and hard to interpret even when predictions stay fine. These are generally accepted statistical definitions.
- Remove one of the pair, keeping the one that is easier to collect or explain.
- Combine them into one feature (a component from PCA, or a domain ratio or difference).
Correlation is computed in Spark ML with `Correlation.corr` (Pearson default).

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Drop one (correct):** the remaining feature keeps almost all the information and the coefficient instability disappears.
- ✗ **B. Mode imputation:** nothing in the question concerns missing values, and the mode of a continuous column is not a fix for collinearity.
- ✗ **C. Spearman:** it is a different way to measure association; computing it does not change the data or remove the dependency.
- ✗ **D. One-hot encoding:** that is for categorical features; numeric columns are not made independent by it.
- ✓ **E. Combine into one (correct):** a principal component or ratio keeps the shared signal in one column and removes the redundancy.

## Key idea
Highly correlated predictors are redundant: drop one or merge them (PCA, ratio) rather than keeping both in a linear model.
Q011415:
## Choosing mean, median or mode
- The **mean** uses every value, so a few extreme values pull it away from a typical row.
- The **median** is the middle value and barely moves when outliers are added, so it is the usual choice for skewed numeric data.
- The **mode** is the most frequent value; it is the natural fill for categorical data.
These are generally accepted statistical definitions.
## In Spark ML
`Imputer` fills missing values with the mean (default), median or mode of the column. The median is computed with `approxQuantile` using a relative error of 0.001.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Mean:** extreme values drag the mean upward, so filled rows would get an unrealistically high income.
- ✓ **B. Median (correct):** it is the middle value, so a handful of very large incomes do not shift it, and it represents a typical household in a skewed column.
- ✗ **C. Mode:** for a continuous income column the most frequent exact value is usually arbitrary (many values appear once) and is not a stable center.
- ✗ **D. Maximum:** it is the most extreme value and would make every filled row an outlier.

## Key idea
Skewed numeric column: impute the median; mean suits symmetric data and mode suits categorical data.
Q011416:
## Imputing categorical data
Mean and median need numbers with a meaningful order and distance. A nominal category such as "card" has neither, so the mean and median of labels are not defined. The mode, the most frequent value, is defined for any data type, so it is the standard simple fill for categorical features. Another option is a separate "missing" category. These are generally accepted data-preparation practices.
## In Spark ML
Spark's `Imputer` supports numeric columns only and documents that it does not support categorical features. For a string column, compute the mode with a `groupBy().count()` and fill with `fillna`.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Mean of counts:** a count is not a label; rounding it cannot produce a valid category.
- ✗ **B. Median of string lengths:** this returns a number, not a payment method, and has no connection to the missing category.
- ✓ **C. Mode (correct):** the most frequent category is a valid label for any categorical column and keeps the column's value set unchanged.
- ✗ **D. Mean of labels:** strings have no meaningful average; alphabetical position would invent an order that does not exist.

## Key idea
Impute categorical features with the mode (or an explicit "missing" category); mean and median are for numeric data.
Q011417:
## Symmetric versus skewed data
For symmetric data the mean, median and mode coincide, so the choice matters little and the mean is cheap and exact. Skew separates them. These are generally accepted statistical facts.
Mean imputation has known side effects: every filled row gets the same value, so the column's variance shrinks and its correlations with other features are weakened. With few missing values these effects are small.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Adds new information:** a constant fill carries no row-specific information; it only avoids dropping the row.
- ✗ **B. Increases variance:** filling with a constant reduces variance because the filled rows sit exactly at the center.
- ✗ **C. Always more robust:** it is the reverse, the median is the robust statistic.
- ✓ **D. Mean and median nearly coincide (correct):** filling with the mean leaves the column's center where it was and is a sensible default when the data are symmetric and have no outliers.

## Key idea
Mean imputation is fine for symmetric data with few gaps, but it shrinks variance; use the median for skewed data.
Q011418:
## What a constant fill does
Replacing every missing value with the mean adds rows exactly at the center. Hence the mean is unchanged, the variance falls (more rows with zero deviation), and the covariance with other features falls too, so correlations are weakened. This is a generally accepted statistical fact, which is why large amounts of missingness call for model-based imputation or an indicator column.
## Spark detail
`Imputer(strategy="mean")` is the default and works on numeric columns only.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Mean unchanged (correct):** adding values equal to the mean does not move the mean of the column.
- ✗ **B. Row-specific values:** mean imputation uses one value for the whole column; neighbor-based fills are a different method.
- ✗ **C. Categorical columns:** a mean of strings is undefined, and Spark's Imputer documents that it does not support categorical features.
- ✗ **D. Strengthens correlations:** a constant carries no co-movement with other features, so correlations weaken.
- ✓ **E. Variance shrinks (correct):** the new rows have zero deviation from the mean, so the spread of the column falls.

## Key idea
Mean imputation keeps the mean, lowers variance and weakens correlations; use it sparingly.
Q011419:
## Leakage in preprocessing
Any statistic learned from data (a median, a mean, a mode) is a parameter of the model pipeline. If it is computed on all rows before the split, the training set contains information about the test rows, and the evaluation no longer simulates unseen data. The generally accepted practice is to split first, compute the fill values on the training set only, and apply those same values to the test set and to new data at serving time.
## In Spark ML
`Imputer` is an estimator: `fit` on the training DataFrame learns the surrogate values, and the resulting model's `transform` applies them to any other DataFrame.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Type change:** splitting rows only separates the rows into two DataFrames and does not change any column type, so it cannot explain a leak or an optimistic score.
- ✓ **B. Leakage (correct):** the median came from all rows including test rows, so the test set influenced the preprocessing; fitting only on training data removes the leak.
- ✗ **C. Cannot split after imputation:** Spark can split any DataFrame at any time with `randomSplit`.
- ✗ **D. Always inflates:** there is no inflation when the statistic is fitted on the training data only.

## Key idea
Fit imputation statistics on the training data only and reuse them on test and serving data.
Q011420:
## How Imputer works
`Imputer` is an estimator. `fit` computes one surrogate value per input column from the non-missing values, using the configured strategy (`mean` default, `median` or `mode`), and returns an `ImputerModel`. `transform` writes the surrogate into the output column wherever the input equals the missing value. The default missing value is `NaN`, and the documentation says all `null` values in the input columns are treated as missing too.
- Median is calculated with `approxQuantile` and a relative error of 0.001.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Zero:** no zero is used; the surrogate is computed from the data unless `setMissingValue` changes what counts as missing.
- ✗ **B. Null stays null:** the documentation states that all nulls in the input columns are treated as missing and are imputed.
- ✓ **C. Median for both (correct):** the strategy is median, and null and NaN are both treated as missing, so both are replaced by the median of the remaining values.
- ✗ **D. Mean:** the strategy was explicitly set to median; the mean is only the default when no strategy is given.

## Key idea
Imputer replaces NaN and null with the mean, median or mode of the non-missing numeric values, using the strategy you set.
Q011421:
## Sentinel values
Some systems write a placeholder such as `-999` instead of null. By default Imputer treats only `NaN` and `null` as missing, so the placeholder would be treated as a real value and would distort the median. The `missingValue` parameter changes which value is regarded as missing (the docs show `setMissingValue(0)` imputing every 0). The surrogate is calculated from the other values, excluding the missing ones.
- Always check for sentinel values in the data summary (a minimum of -999 is the hint).

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Mean with missingValue 0:** this would impute genuine zero distances and use the wrong strategy.
- ✗ **B. relativeError:** this parameter controls the accuracy of the approximate median, not which value counts as missing, so the -999 sentinels stay in the data.
- ✗ **C. Mode with defaults:** only NaN/null count as missing, so the sentinels stay and also affect the mode.
- ✓ **D. Median with `missingValue=-999.0` (correct):** it marks the sentinel as missing, computes the median of the genuine distances, and writes it into the new column.

## Key idea
Use `missingValue` to tell Imputer which sentinel (such as -999) means "missing"; NaN and null are always treated as missing.
Q011422:
## Imputer and strings
Spark's `Imputer` input columns should be numeric. The documentation says it does not support categorical features and may create incorrect values for them, even with `strategy="mode"`.
For a string column do it by hand: count each value, take the most frequent non-null one (for example `df.groupBy("city").count().orderBy("count", ascending=False)`), and fill with `df.fillna({"city": top_city})`. If the column is going to be one-hot encoded afterwards, `StringIndexer` with `handleInvalid="keep"` is another way to give missing values their own index.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. missingValue empty string:** that only changes which numeric value counts as missing; it does not make the input type accepted.
- ✗ **B. Mean strategy:** mean is not defined for strings, and Imputer does not support categorical features for any strategy.
- ✓ **C. groupBy plus fillna (correct):** this finds the real mode of the strings and writes it into the missing rows, which Imputer cannot do for text.
- ✗ **D. Cast to float:** strings such as city names become null on a cast, losing all information and imputing nothing meaningful.

## Key idea
Imputer is numeric-only; impute a categorical string column with its mode using a groupBy count and `fillna`.
Q011423:
## Estimator and model
`Imputer` is an estimator: calling `fit` on the training data learns a surrogate value per column and returns an `ImputerModel` (a transformer). The model stores those learned values and later `transform` calls only apply them. This keeps preprocessing consistent between training and serving, and it avoids leakage because the scoring data never influences the fill value.
- If the scoring batch had its own median computed, the same row could be filled differently on different days and in a different batch composition than in training.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Recompute at scoring:** a transformer does not learn; only `fit` computes statistics.
- ✓ **B. Learned training median (correct):** the `ImputerModel` keeps the surrogate values from `fit`, so new batches are filled with the same values used in training.
- ✗ **C. Mean of the batch:** the strategy was median and values come from training, not from the batch.
- ✗ **D. Works only in training:** a fitted model's `transform` is what runs at scoring time.

## Key idea
Fit once on training data; the ImputerModel reuses the stored values for every later batch.
Q011424:
## Imputer facts
From the Spark documentation: Imputer is an estimator that completes missing values using the mean, median or mode of the columns where values are missing. Input columns must be numeric; categorical features are not supported. The default `strategy` is `mean`. All nulls are treated as missing, and `missingValue` (default NaN) can be changed. The statistic is computed after filtering out missing values.
- Because it is an estimator, you call `fit` first and use the resulting `ImputerModel` to `transform`.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Mean, median and mode on numeric columns (correct):** this matches the documented behavior, with mean the default strategy.
- ✗ **B. Mean only on any type:** median and mode are supported, and categorical columns are not.
- ✗ **C. Transformer without fit:** Imputer is an estimator whose `fit` computes the surrogate values.
- ✗ **D. Median default on strings:** the default is mean, and string columns are not supported.

## Key idea
Imputer: numeric columns, strategy mean (default), median or mode; fit then transform.
Q011425:
## Why nominal categories are not integers
A linear model multiplies a feature by one weight. If `colour` is a single integer, the model assumes green is "between" red and blue, and that the effect of moving from 0 to 2 is twice that from 0 to 1. For a nominal category that is false.
One-hot encoding gives each category its own 0/1 column (or a vector with a single 1), so each category can have its own weight. The Spark documentation notes that this encoding lets algorithms that expect continuous features, such as logistic regression, use categorical features. The ordering problem is a generally accepted modeling fact.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Implied order and spacing (correct):** with integer codes the model sees ordered, equally spaced numbers; one-hot columns let each colour carry its own coefficient.
- ✗ **B. Cannot read numerics:** logistic regression works on numeric inputs; the issue is the meaning of the numbers.
- ✗ **C. Memory:** one-hot vectors use more space, not less, and the reason for encoding is correctness.
- ✗ **D. Normal distribution:** indicator columns are binary, so they are not normally distributed.

## Key idea
Nominal categories should be one-hot encoded for linear models so no false order or spacing is implied.
Q011426:
## From strings to a feature vector
`OneHotEncoder` expects category indices as input, not strings. The Spark documentation says that for string data it is common to encode categories with `StringIndexer` first. Its output vector column is then commonly merged with the numeric columns into one vector with `VectorAssembler`.
- `StringIndexer` maps `country` to an index (most frequent first by default).
- `OneHotEncoder` turns the index into a binary vector.
- `VectorAssembler` combines the encoded vector with `age` and `income` into a `features` column.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Encoder before indexer:** the encoder would receive raw strings, which it does not accept.
- ✗ **B. Assembler first:** the assembler would receive a string column and have nothing numeric to combine for `country`.
- ✗ **C. Assembler before encoder:** the indices would be merged as plain numbers into the vector before they are one-hot encoded, so the category would be treated as an ordered value.
- ✓ **D. Index, encode, assemble (correct):** each stage consumes the previous output, ending with one feature vector for the estimator.

## Key idea
StringIndexer, then OneHotEncoder, then VectorAssembler.
Q011427:
## The dropLast default
The Spark documentation explains that the last category is not included by default (`dropLast=True`) because including it would make the entries of each vector sum to one, which are linearly dependent. With 5 categories the output length is therefore 4: index 2 maps to `[0, 0, 1, 0]`, and index 4 (the last category) maps to `[0, 0, 0, 0]`.
- Set `dropLast=False` to keep a full length-5 vector.
- Tree-based and linear models can both use the reduced form; the missing category is represented by "all zeros".

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Single 4.0:** that would be the original index, not a one-hot vector.
- ✓ **B. All zeros of length 4 (correct):** dropLast is true by default, so the final category is the baseline with no indicator.
- ✗ **C. All ones:** a one-hot vector has at most one entry equal to one.
- ✗ **D. Length 5:** that is the result of `dropLast=False`, which was not set.

## Key idea
Default `dropLast=True` gives N-1 columns; the last category is all zeros.
Q011428:
## Unseen categories
`StringIndexer` is fitted on training data and knows only the labels it saw. Its `handleInvalid` parameter defaults to `error`, so unseen labels throw an exception at transform time. Other options are `skip` (drop the row) and `keep` (put unseen labels at an extra index equal to the number of labels).
`OneHotEncoder` also has `handleInvalid` with `error` (default) and `keep`; with `keep` an extra category is added as the last one, so with `dropLast=True` invalid values become an all-zero vector.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Lower case:** this affects spelling only, and a truly new country would still be unseen.
- ✗ **B. Drop the encoder:** the model was trained with encoded features and would receive a different input.
- ✓ **C. handleInvalid="keep" (correct):** unseen countries are mapped to an extra index and encoded instead of raising an error, so the batch is still scored.
- ✗ **D. dropLast:** it changes how many columns the vector has and does not affect how unknown labels are handled.

## Key idea
Use handleInvalid="keep" so unseen categories get an extra index instead of failing; "skip" would drop the rows.
Q011429:
## What OneHotEncoder does
From the Spark documentation: `OneHotEncoder` maps a categorical feature represented as a label index to a binary vector with at most a single one-value, allowing algorithms that expect continuous features, such as logistic regression, to use categorical features. It can transform multiple columns and returns one output vector column for each input column; the outputs are usually merged with `VectorAssembler`. For strings, index them with `StringIndexer` first. `handleInvalid` is `error` or `keep`, and `dropLast` defaults to `True`.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Multiple columns (correct):** the encoder accepts `inputCols` and `outputCols` lists and returns a vector column for each input.
- ✗ **B. Mean imputation:** that is `Imputer`; the encoder does not fill missing values.
- ✗ **C. Raw strings:** the encoder takes category indices, so strings must go through `StringIndexer` first.
- ✗ **D. Keeps all categories:** `dropLast=True` by default, so the last category is omitted.
- ✓ **E. Index to binary vector (correct):** that is the definition; at most one entry is one.

## Key idea
OneHotEncoder turns indexed categories into binary vectors, handles many columns at once, drops the last category by default and needs StringIndexer for strings.
Q011430:
## Libraries on Databricks
The Databricks tuning page lists three Python libraries that scale across several machines to find good hyperparameters with little manual orchestration.
- **Optuna**: light-weight, with dynamic search spaces; parallelized with Joblib, or with parallel studies on Spark through MLflow 3 classes; trials tracked in MLflow.
- **Ray Tune**: comes with Ray, which Databricks Runtime ML includes, and uses Ray as the backend for distributed computing.
- **Hyperopt**: legacy. Open-source Hyperopt is no longer maintained and is not included in Databricks Runtime for Machine Learning after 16.4 LTS ML.
## Not a tuning library
`CrossValidator` and `ParamGridBuilder` belong to Spark ML: they evaluate a fixed grid for Spark ML pipelines and do not run on Ray.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Optuna:** a valid tuning library, but its scaling comes from Joblib or Spark executors, not from a Ray backend.
- ✗ **B. CrossValidator:** it is a Spark ML grid tool whose fits run as Spark jobs; it has no Ray integration and no adaptive search.
- ✗ **C. Hyperopt:** its distribution goes through Spark tasks, not Ray, and it is unmaintained and dropped from the runtime after 16.4 LTS ML.
- ✓ **D. Ray Tune (correct):** it is built on Ray, so it reuses the Ray cluster that Databricks Runtime ML already provides, and the Databricks docs name it as a replacement for the distributed Hyperopt experience.

## Key idea
Ray Tune = tuning on a Ray backend; Optuna = dynamic spaces with Joblib or Spark; Hyperopt = legacy.
Q011431:
## Two kinds of workloads
- A **single-machine** model (scikit-learn, for example) trains on one node. Running many trials at once means sending trials to different workers.
- A **distributed** algorithm (Spark MLlib, Horovod) already spreads one training run over the whole cluster.
## Do not stack parallelism
Running many trials of an already distributed trainer at the same time makes them compete for the same executors, so there is no speed-up. The Databricks Hyperopt docs state the same rule for the legacy tool: use `SparkTrials` for single-machine models and the default sequential `Trials` class for MLlib or Horovod, because model building is already parallel. The rule is about workload type, not about the library, so it carries over to Optuna.
## Legacy status
Hyperopt and `SparkTrials` are not included in Databricks Runtime for Machine Learning after 16.4 LTS ML; Databricks recommends Optuna or Ray Tune.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Switch to scikit-learn:** this is a different algorithm that must fit in memory on the driver, so a very large DataFrame cannot be used and the results change.
- ✓ **B. Sequential trials (correct):** an MLlib fit is already parallelized across executors, so trials run one at a time and each fit uses the full cluster.
- ✗ **C. Concurrent distributed fits:** a Spark task on a worker cannot start another distributed job, and the fits would compete for the same executors anyway.
- ✗ **D. Copy per trial:** duplicating the data multiplies storage and memory use, while the contention is for executor cores, which copies do not add.

## Key idea
Distributed trainer (MLlib) → run trials sequentially; single-node trainer → distribute the trials.
Q011432:
## Define-by-run search spaces
In Optuna you write an `objective(trial)` function. Inside it you ask the `trial` object for values: `suggest_float`, `suggest_int`, `suggest_categorical`. The search space is therefore declared as the code runs, which lets the space depend on earlier choices (for example, `SVR` parameters only if `SVR` was chosen). The function returns the value to optimize.
## On Databricks
Optuna is one of the libraries the Databricks tuning page lists (with Ray Tune and Hyperopt). It integrates with MLflow to track hyperparameters and metrics, and can be parallelized with Joblib or with parallel studies on Spark.
- Hyperopt declares the space outside the function (`hp.uniform`, `hp.choice`) and passes it as `space` to `fmin()`. It is legacy on recent runtimes.
- `ParamGridBuilder` and `GridSearchCV` take explicit lists of values, not suggestions.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Hyperopt:** its space is passed in as a `space` argument built with `hp` functions; there are no `trial.suggest_*` calls, and Hyperopt is legacy on recent runtimes.
- ✗ **B. ParamGridBuilder:** it builds a fixed grid with `addGrid(param, [values])`; it has no suggest calls and no search algorithm that adapts to results.
- ✓ **C. Optuna (correct):** `trial.suggest_*` calls inside the objective function define the search space dynamically, and Optuna integrates with MLflow for tracking.
- ✗ **D. GridSearchCV:** it takes an estimator and a dictionary of explicit value lists and tries every combination; there is no objective function with a trial object.

## Key idea
Optuna = objective(trial) with suggest_* calls; Hyperopt = fmin(fn, space, algo, max_evals) and is legacy.
Q011433:
## Why parallel Optuna needs shared storage
Each trial needs to know about the results of other trials, so parallel workers must read and write the same study state. Optuna stores it in a storage backend. In MLflow 3, `MlflowStorage` lets Optuna use the MLflow tracking server as that backend, with batching to avoid REST API throttling.
## Running studies on Spark
`MlflowSparkStudy` wraps an Optuna study so that `optimize(objective, n_trials=8, n_jobs=4)` launches parallel studies on PySpark executors. By default it uses the `TPESampler` and the `MedianPruner` (which stops unpromising trials early).
## Legacy names
`SparkTrials` and `fmin()` belong to Hyperopt, which is not included in Databricks Runtime for Machine Learning after 16.4 LTS ML.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. CrossValidator:** a Spark MLlib class that evaluates a fixed grid with k-fold validation; it is not part of Optuna and does not run Optuna studies.
- ✗ **B. SparkTrials:** this class belongs to Hyperopt's `fmin()`; `optuna.create_study` does not accept it.
- ✗ **C. fmin with tpe.suggest:** `fmin()` is the Hyperopt entry point; Optuna starts a run with a study's `optimize`. TPE is the default Optuna sampler, so no wrapper is needed.
- ✓ **D. MlflowStorage (correct):** it gives parallel workers one shared Optuna storage in the MLflow tracking server, so every trial result is visible to all of them and logged in the experiment.
- ✓ **E. MlflowSparkStudy (correct):** its `optimize` method runs the Optuna study in parallel on Spark executors, using `n_trials` and `n_jobs`.

## Key idea
Parallel Optuna on Databricks = MlflowStorage for shared state plus MlflowSparkStudy to run the study on executors.
Q011434:
## Hyperopt status
The Databricks tuning page states that open-source Hyperopt is no longer maintained and that it is not included in Databricks Runtime for Machine Learning after 16.4 LTS ML. Notebooks that import `hyperopt` or `SparkTrials` on a newer runtime need a replacement.
## What the docs recommend
- **Optuna**: light-weight, dynamic search spaces, MLflow integration, parallel studies on Spark.
- **Ray Tune**: part of Ray on Databricks; the docs point to it for a similar experience to the deprecated distributed Hyperopt tuning.
- MLlib's `CrossValidator` and `TrainValidationSplit` remain valid for Spark ML pipelines, but they are grid-based tools for MLlib, not a drop-in replacement for tuning single-node models.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. AutoML only:** AutoML is a separate feature for quick baselines; the tuning libraries are fully supported and documented.
- ✗ **B. CrossValidator only:** it suits Spark ML pipelines and grid search, but the docs list Optuna and Ray Tune for tuning general (for example scikit-learn) models.
- ✓ **C. Optuna or Ray Tune (correct):** the Databricks docs recommend them as replacements, and Optuna can run parallel studies on Spark.
- ✗ **D. Rewritten Hyperopt:** nothing is rewritten; the open-source project is unmaintained and the library is dropped from the runtime after 16.4 LTS ML.

## Key idea
Hyperopt (fmin, SparkTrials) is legacy; use Optuna or Ray Tune for scalable tuning.
Q011435:
## Cost of a grid
A grid tries every combination: 6 hyperparameters with 8 values each give 8^6 = 262,144 runs. The count multiplies with every added hyperparameter, so grids are practical only for few hyperparameters with a few values each.
## Fixed budgets
- **Random search** draws each setting from a distribution. The budget is whatever you choose (60 trials), and every trial tests a new value for every hyperparameter, which matters because usually only a few hyperparameters strongly affect the result.
- **Bayesian optimization** (for example TPE, the default Optuna sampler) also has a chosen number of trials but uses earlier results to pick promising settings.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Exhaustive grid:** 262,144 runs of 20 minutes each is about ten years of compute, which does not fit a budget of 60 runs.
- ✓ **B. (correct):** A budget of 60 trials works with random search or Bayesian optimization, because their cost is a number you set rather than a product of grid sizes.
- ✗ **C. First two only:** leaving four hyperparameters at defaults may leave the most influential ones untuned and ignores the budget logic.
- ✗ **D. Two values each:** 2^6 = 64 combinations fits the budget, but two points per axis explore very little and could miss the best region; sampled values explore six dimensions more thoroughly. A grid also has no guarantee of better coverage.

## Key idea
Many hyperparameters and a fixed budget → random or Bayesian search; grid search only for a few small dimensions.
Q011436:
## Three search strategies
- **Grid search**: every combination from lists of values.
- **Random search**: each trial is drawn independently from the space, so trials can run in any order, all at once.
- **Bayesian optimization**: builds a model of how the loss depends on the hyperparameters (TPE in Hyperopt and Optuna's default sampler) and uses it to propose the next trial. The next suggestion depends on the results so far.
## Trade-off
Bayesian methods usually need fewer trials to find a good region, but their sequential nature limits how many trials can be useful in parallel, which is covered in the parallelism questions.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Adaptive suggestions (correct):** the optimizer learns from completed trials and proposes settings in regions that gave low loss, which often reaches better results than independent samples in the same number of trials.
- ✗ **B. No objective function:** every tuner needs one, because the loss is measured by training and evaluating a model.
- ✗ **C. Enumerate first:** that describes grid search; a Bayesian optimizer never enumerates all combinations.
- ✗ **D. Independent sampling:** that describes random search; the whole point of Bayesian optimization is to use past results.

## Key idea
Random search = independent draws; Bayesian (TPE) = next trial chosen from past results.
Q011437:
## Scale of a hyperparameter
Some hyperparameters (regularization strength, learning rate, SVM `C`) act on a multiplicative scale: the difference between 0.0001 and 0.001 matters as much as between 10 and 100.
- A **uniform** distribution over 0.00001 to 100 puts about 90 percent of draws above 10, so the small values are almost never tried.
- A **log-uniform** distribution samples the exponent uniformly, so every power of ten gets equal attention. In Optuna this is `suggest_float(..., log=True)`; Hyperopt offered `hp.loguniform` (legacy).
- Integers such as tree depth use an integer range (`suggest_int`).

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Three categories:** it removes the ability to find a value between the choices, such as 0.01, and loses the continuous range the search should explore.
- ✗ **B. Integers 1 to 100:** it excludes every value below 1, which is where the lower part of the range lies.
- ✗ **C. Uniform:** nearly all draws land at large values, so the small-regularization region where many models perform best is barely sampled.
- ✓ **D. Log scale (correct):** it distributes trials evenly over the orders of magnitude, so values near 0.00001 are explored as often as values near 10. The Databricks Optuna example uses `log=True` for the SVR `C` parameter.

## Key idea
Scale-type hyperparameters (regularization, learning rate, C) → sample on a log scale.
Q011438:
## When a grid is fine
Grid cost is the product of the number of values per hyperparameter. With 3 x 4 x 2 = 24 combinations and seconds per fit, an exhaustive grid is cheap, deterministic (no sampling randomness) and gives complete coverage of the listed values. Spark MLlib's `ParamGridBuilder` and scikit-learn's `GridSearchCV` are built for exactly this.
## When it is not
The product grows quickly: adding a hyperparameter with 10 values multiplies the cost by 10, and the grid wastes trials if only one hyperparameter matters.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. One trial per parameter:** a single trial cannot test three or four values of each hyperparameter, and combinations are never explored.
- ✓ **B. Grid search (correct):** 24 combinations of short fits is affordable, and it tests every listed combination exactly once with no randomness.
- ✗ **C. Five random trials:** fewer than a quarter of the combinations are sampled, and the number of trials has no general relation to generalization.
- ✗ **D. Bayesian covers all:** Bayesian optimization is adaptive and concentrates on promising regions; it does not guarantee every combination is tested.

## Key idea
Few hyperparameters, few values, cheap fits → grid search; large spaces → random or Bayesian.
Q011439:
## Two ways to use a cluster
- **Distribute one training run** (MLlib, Horovod): useful when the data or model is too large for one machine.
- **Distribute many independent runs** of a single-node model: each trial is one model fit with one hyperparameter setting, so many can run at once on different workers. This is the right pattern when the data fits on a node and tuning is the slow part.
## Tools
On current runtimes, Databricks recommends Optuna (parallel studies on Spark executors) and Ray Tune. The legacy Hyperopt `SparkTrials` class worked the same way: the driver generated trials and workers evaluated them as one-task Spark jobs.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. 32 folds:** folds multiply the total work (each setting is fit 32 times) rather than spreading the existing work, and a fold count is a validation design choice, not a parallelism setting.
- ✗ **B. Sequential on the driver:** a single-node model does not need to be distributed to parallelize the search; trials are independent fits.
- ✓ **C. Distributed trial runners (correct):** 32 cores can evaluate up to 32 single-node fits at once, which cuts a 200-trial search from about 13 hours of sequential work to a small fraction of it, with the same model.
- ✗ **D. Switch to MLlib:** a different library gives a different algorithm implementation and different results; it is a rewrite, not a transparent optimization.

## Key idea
Single-node model + many trials → distribute trials across workers (Optuna on Spark, Ray Tune), not the model.
Q011440:
## Parallelism versus adaptivity
An adaptive optimizer proposes the next setting from the completed trials. With 64 trials running at the same time, the first 64 suggestions are made with almost no results available, which makes them close to random. Only later rounds benefit from the history.
The Databricks Hyperopt docs state it directly: for a fixed number of evaluations, greater parallelism speeds up the computation, while lower parallelism may lead to better results because each iteration has access to more past results. The same logic holds for any Bayesian tool.
## Practical choice
- Random search and grid search do not depend on earlier results, so they scale to full parallelism with no loss of quality.
- For Bayesian search, choose moderate concurrency, such as a handful of trials, and run enough rounds for learning to occur.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Fewer past results per suggestion (correct):** with many simultaneous trials, the optimizer sees less history at each decision, so it behaves more like random search; this is the speed versus adaptivity trade-off.
- ✗ **B. Switch to grid:** optimizers do not change algorithm based on concurrency; the sampler stays Bayesian.
- ✗ **C. Less data per trial:** each trial trains on the same dataset; parallelism does not subsample the data.
- ✗ **D. Fewer trials:** the budget is fixed at 128 for both settings; concurrency changes how they are scheduled, not how many run.

## Key idea
More parallel trials = faster but less adaptive for Bayesian search; random search has no such cost.
Q011441:
## Many small models
When each model is small but there are thousands of them, parallelism comes from the grouping, not from a distributed algorithm. `groupBy(...).applyInPandas(func, schema)` groups the Spark DataFrame, hands each group as a pandas DataFrame to the function, which can fit a scikit-learn model (and even tune it with a small search) and return a result as a DataFrame. Spark runs the groups as tasks in parallel across executors.
## What to return
The function usually returns metrics and hyperparameters per group (and can log to MLflow). Heavy models are saved to storage or logged, not returned in the DataFrame.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. applyInPandas by store (correct):** Spark spreads the groups over executors, so many single-node models are trained concurrently, each with its own store's data.
- ✗ **B. Driver loop:** all work runs on one machine, one store at a time, which wastes the cluster.
- ✗ **C. One MLlib model:** it fits one global model; the request is for a separate model per store, and a numeric id would be treated as an ordinal feature.
- ✗ **D. Fit once with store_id as label:** this turns the stores into classes of a single classification problem and does not forecast per store.

## Key idea
One small single-node model per group → groupBy().applyInPandas() runs the groups in parallel.
Q011442:
## What runs where
Parallel trials execute the objective function on worker tasks. Spark DataFrames and the SparkSession belong to the driver, so using `spark.table(...)` inside a worker task fails or triggers nested jobs. Single-node tuning code needs data in plain Python form on the worker: a pandas/NumPy array, a Parquet or Delta path it can read, or a broadcast variable.
## Practical guidance
Each trial is evaluated in a task on a worker. When data is large, put it on shared storage and read it in the objective, or pass a small training sample. If the data does not fit on a worker at all, use a distributed algorithm instead (for example MLlib) and tune sequentially.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Run the objective on the driver:** that removes the parallelism that the team wants and does not solve the 40 GB read.
- ✗ **B. Large parallelism:** the problem is where the data access happens; more concurrent tasks repeat the failing read.
- ✓ **C. Make the data readable by workers (correct):** reading from a storage path (or broadcasting a small sample) works in worker tasks, while the Spark session does not.
- ✗ **D. More driver memory:** workers do not read the driver's memory; a bigger driver does not make a session usable from worker tasks.

## Key idea
Trial functions run on workers: give them data through storage paths or broadcasts, not the SparkSession.
Q011443:
## How trials map to cluster resources
A trial corresponds to fitting one model with one hyperparameter setting. In the documented SparkTrials design, the driver generates trials and each is evaluated in one Spark task on a worker; if a worker can run several tasks, several trials run on it at once. The requested parallelism is reduced to the number of concurrent tasks the cluster allows.
- Scaling is bounded by cores (task slots): extra trials queue.
- Single-node models do not become distributed by wrapping them in a Pipeline; a Pipeline is an MLlib construct for MLlib estimators.
- Adaptive searchers can return different results at different concurrency, because suggestions depend on completed trials.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Wrap in Pipeline:** a Pipeline chains MLlib stages and does not distribute scikit-learn fits.
- ✗ **B. Always the same result:** with Bayesian methods the suggestions depend on earlier results, so higher concurrency changes the sequence and can change the best result.
- ✗ **C. No limit:** queued trials wait for free slots, so more parallelism than slots gives nothing; the cluster size is the cap.
- ✓ **D. Task slots limit (correct):** trials are evaluated as tasks, so only as many trials run at once as the cluster has free task slots.
- ✓ **E. Independent fits (correct):** because every trial is its own fit, distributing trials needs no change to the model code and runs them concurrently on workers.

## Key idea
Parallel trials = independent fits on task slots; capacity is capped by cores, and adaptive optimizers lose some adaptivity.
Q011444:
## Cost versus reliability
- **Train-validation split** (`TrainValidationSplit`): one split (for example `trainRatio=0.8`). Each parameter setting is fit and evaluated once, so the cost is one fit per setting. The estimate depends on one random split, which is a problem for small datasets.
- **k-fold cross-validation** (`CrossValidator`): the data is split into k folds, each setting is fit k times and the metrics are averaged. The estimate is steadier but costs k times more. After choosing the best settings, both methods refit on the whole dataset.
## Choosing
With very large data, a single validation set of millions of rows is a stable estimate, so the cheaper single split is the sensible trade. With small data, k-fold is worth the extra cost.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Two folds equal a split:** two-fold CV fits twice per setting and averages swapped roles, so it costs double and uses 50 percent training data per fit, not a train/validation ratio.
- ✓ **B. TrainValidationSplit (correct):** a single validation split holding tens of millions of the 600 million rows is statistically reliable, and it is about k times cheaper than k-fold.
- ✗ **C. Ten folds always:** ten folds multiplies the grid cost by ten, and with so much data the extra reliability is not needed.
- ✗ **D. No validation:** scoring on training data rewards memorization and cannot select among hyperparameters.

## Key idea
Large data + limited budget → single train-validation split; small data → k-fold for a steadier estimate.
Q011445:
## Variance of a single split
With 900 rows, an 80/20 split gives 180 validation rows. The measured accuracy depends on which rows landed there; one point of difference (about two rows of 180) can be luck. A different random split could reverse the ranking.
## What k-fold does
k-fold splits data into k parts, trains k times (each part is validation once, the rest is training), and averages. Every row is used for both training and validation across folds, and the average has lower variance than one split. The price is k times the training cost, acceptable for small data.
## Limits
Cross-validation estimates generalization to similar data; it does not guarantee future performance, and a final held-out test set is still good practice.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. No test set:** CV is used for model selection; a final unseen test set is still used for an honest final estimate.
- ✗ **B. Trains once:** it trains k times, so it costs more than a single split.
- ✗ **C. Guarantee:** an average over folds is an estimate, and it does not promise the best accuracy on new data.
- ✓ **D. Averaging over folds (correct):** the metric comes from k different validation sets (every row validates once), so a one-point gap is far less likely to be noise.

## Key idea
Small data → k-fold for a steadier estimate, at k times the cost; huge data → one split.
Q011446:
## Order matters in time series
Random k-fold assumes rows are independent. In daily sales, neighboring days are strongly correlated and trends continue. When a validation day from March is scored by a model that trained on April rows, the model has effectively seen the future and the neighborhood of the target.
## Better validation
Use a split that respects time: train on the past and validate on a later period, repeated with a moving (expanding or rolling) window. In scikit-learn this is `TimeSeriesSplit`; with a train-validation split, split by a date cutoff rather than at random.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Cannot validate:** time series can be validated with time-ordered splits.
- ✗ **B. Random k-fold overfits always:** random k-fold works well for independent rows. The issue is the dependence between rows ordered in time.
- ✓ **C. Leakage from the future (correct):** random folds mix time periods, so validation rows are close to training rows in time and the model looks better than it will on truly future data.
- ✗ **D. Too few folds:** the number of folds sets the training share per fit, not whether future data is used; adding folds does not remove time leakage.

## Key idea
Time-ordered data → validate on later periods (time-aware splits), not random folds.
Q011447:
## Comparing the two
- **Fits per setting**: split 1, k-fold k.
- **Validation data**: split one fixed subset, k-fold each row once across k subsets.
- **Estimate**: split depends on the split, k-fold is averaged and steadier.
- **Best for**: split big data and tight budgets, k-fold small or medium data.
Both can be combined with a grid or a search, and both usually refit the best settings on the full training data.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Cannot combine with a grid:** `CrossValidator` takes `estimatorParamMaps`, the grid, as a core argument.
- ✓ **B. k times the cost (correct):** each setting is fit once per fold (the Spark docs call cross-validation over a grid "very expensive"; k of 3 or 10 are common).
- ✗ **C. Always better:** more training rows in the single split do not change which hyperparameters are best; the noisier estimate may even pick a worse one.
- ✗ **D. Lower variance:** a single fixed subset gives a noisier estimate, not a steadier one.
- ✓ **E. Every row validates once (correct):** averaging k metrics reduces the dependence on a single validation subset.

## Key idea
k-fold = k times the cost for a steadier estimate; single split = cheap but noisier.
Q011448:
## Class imbalance and folds
With 2,000 rows and 0.5 percent fraud, there are about 10 positive rows in total, or 2 per fold. A random split can easily give one fold zero positives, making recall or AUC undefined or extreme.
## Stratified folds
Stratified k-fold splits each class separately so every fold keeps the original class proportions. In scikit-learn `StratifiedKFold` (and `cross_val_score` for classifiers uses it by default for integer `cv`). This stabilizes fold metrics but does not create more positive rows; a metric such as precision-recall AUC and class weights are still needed (see the imbalance questions).

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Stratified folds (correct):** each fold has about the same fraction of fraud rows, so every validation set can score the positive class.
- ✗ **B. Sort by label:** contiguous label blocks put all positives into one fold and none in the rest, which is the worst case.
- ✗ **C. Only fraud rows:** scoring only positives makes precision and accuracy meaningless because false positives can never occur.
- ✗ **D. One fold:** k-fold needs at least two folds; a single fold would give no validation split and hides the variation instead of reducing it.

## Key idea
Imbalanced classes → stratified folds so each fold has the class ratio.
Q011449:
## Anatomy of CrossValidator
`CrossValidator` needs three things (the Spark ML tuning guide):
- an **`Estimator`**: the algorithm or a whole `Pipeline` to tune;
- a set of **`ParamMap`s** (`estimatorParamMaps`), usually built with `ParamGridBuilder().addGrid(lr.regParam, [0.01, 0.1]).build()`;
- an **`Evaluator`**, such as `BinaryClassificationEvaluator`, `MulticlassClassificationEvaluator` or `RegressionEvaluator`, which supplies the metric that ranks the parameter maps (`setMetricName` overrides the default).
`numFolds` sets k. `fit(train_df)` returns a `CrossValidatorModel`; `bestModel` is refit with the best parameter map on the whole training data.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Estimator, grid, evaluator (correct):** these are the three required items, plus `numFolds` (the default is 3).
- ✗ **B. Trained model:** `CrossValidator` fits the models itself on each fold; it takes an untrained estimator.
- ✗ **C. Table and key:** folds are made by random split of the DataFrame passed to `fit`, not from table keys.
- ✗ **D. Only a DataFrame:** the DataFrame is given to `fit`, but the estimator, grid and metric must be configured.

## Key idea
CrossValidator(estimator, estimatorParamMaps, evaluator, numFolds); fit returns a model refit on the best parameters.
Q011450:
## Leakage through preprocessing
If the scaler is fit on all training rows, the mean and standard deviation of each validation fold have influenced the scaling that the model receives. The effect is usually small, but with imputers, target encoders, feature selection or PCA the leak can be large.
## The fix
An `Estimator` handed to `CrossValidator` can be a `Pipeline`. The tuner then fits the whole pipeline on the training folds of each split, so every fitted stage (scaler, imputer, indexer) learns only from training rows and is applied to the held-out fold. The same idea in scikit-learn is passing a `Pipeline` to `GridSearchCV` or `cross_val_score`.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Fit on validation fold:** a transformer must learn only from training data, otherwise the validation labels' neighbors influence the transformation.
- ✓ **B. Pipeline as the estimator (correct):** all stages are refit inside each fold using only that fold's training rows, which removes preprocessing leakage and also lets pipeline stage parameters join the grid.
- ✗ **C. Fit on everything:** including the test set leaks even more information and makes the final estimate unreliable.
- ✗ **D. Drop the scaler:** scaling affects how regularized logistic regression penalizes features and speeds up convergence, so it matters; removing it changes the model and is not a fix for leakage.

## Key idea
Put preprocessing and model in one Pipeline and give it to the CrossValidator so each fold fits its own transformers.
Q011451:
## cross_val_score
`cross_val_score(estimator, X, y, cv=5, scoring=...)` clones the estimator, fits it on four folds, scores it on the fifth, and repeats for each fold. It returns an array with one score per fold, so `len(scores) == 5`. You typically report `scores.mean()` and `scores.std()`.
## What it does not do
- It does not search hyperparameters: for that use `GridSearchCV`, `RandomizedSearchCV` or a tuner such as Optuna, where each trial can call `cross_val_score` (as in the Databricks Hyperopt example, which uses the mean cross-validation accuracy as the objective).
- It does not return a fitted model; the estimator you passed is not trained.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Pooled score:** each fold is scored separately; the folds are not combined into one metric.
- ✗ **B. Fitted forest:** no model is returned, and there is no hyperparameter search in this call.
- ✗ **C. Confusion matrices:** the output is the chosen scoring metric, F1, not a matrix.
- ✓ **D. Array of per-fold scores (correct):** one F1 for each of the five validation folds, with the mean as the summary.

## Key idea
cross_val_score returns one score per fold; it does not tune or return a model.
Q011452:
## Serial by default
The Spark ML guide says that by default parameter sets from the grid are evaluated in serial. Setting `parallelism` to 2 or more on `CrossValidator` or `TrainValidationSplit` evaluates models in parallel. The value should be chosen to use the cluster without exceeding its resources; larger values do not always help, and a value up to 10 is usually enough for most clusters.
## Cost reminder
The grid has 3 x 2 = 6 settings and 3 folds, so 18 model fits, plus one refit of the best model on all data. Parallelism makes the same work finish sooner but does not reduce it.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Collect to the driver:** collecting the data discards the cluster and may exceed driver memory.
- ✗ **B. numFolds 1:** cross-validation needs at least two folds, and lowering the number of folds changes the validation instead of speeding up the same work.
- ✓ **C. Set parallelism (correct):** it lets several parameter-and-fold fits run concurrently on available cluster resources, while the fit count stays 18.
- ✗ **D. Driver loop:** a loop on the driver is serial and loses MLlib's distributed fitting.

## Key idea
CrossValidator runs serially by default; raise `parallelism` (moderately) to evaluate fits concurrently.
Q011453:
## What fit() does
For each parameter map, `CrossValidator` fits the estimator on each of the k training splits and evaluates each model on the held-out fold. The score of a parameter map is the mean of its k fold metrics. After finding the best map, it fits the estimator again with that map on the whole dataset passed to `fit` (the Spark docs: "`CrossValidator` finally re-fits the `Estimator` using the best `ParamMap` and the entire dataset"). That final model is `bestModel`.
## Where the test set fits
The test DataFrame never enters `fit`. After tuning, you evaluate `cv_model.transform(test_df)` once to estimate generalization.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Refit on test:** the test DataFrame is not passed to `fit` and must stay unseen until the final evaluation.
- ✗ **B. Fit on validation fold:** this reverses the roles; each model is fitted on the training folds and scored on the held-out fold.
- ✓ **C. Refit on all training data (correct):** `bestModel` is trained again with the best parameter map on the full DataFrame given to `fit`, so the final model uses every training row.
- ✗ **D. First fold only:** all k models for each map are fitted and evaluated; the final model is a new fit.
- ✓ **E. Mean of k fold metrics (correct):** each parameter map's score is averaged over its k fitted models, and the best average wins.

## Key idea
CrossValidator averages k fold metrics per parameter map, then refits the best map on all training data.
Q011454:
## Why random search covers important dimensions better
In a grid with 3 values per hyperparameter, every trial reuses one of only 3 values of each important hyperparameter, however many trials are run. In random search each trial draws a fresh value, so 80 trials test 80 different values of each important hyperparameter. When only a few of many hyperparameters matter, which is common, the same budget explores the influential axes far more densely.
## When a grid is still fine
For two or three hyperparameters with few values and fast fits, an exhaustive grid is acceptable (see the grid question). Bayesian methods such as TPE go further by using results to focus the draws.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Distinct values per trial (correct):** random draws give 80 different values of each important hyperparameter, while the grid repeats 3 values.
- ✗ **B. More epochs:** the training budget per trial is a separate setting; the search strategy does not change it.
- ✗ **C. Ignore hyperparameters:** every hyperparameter still gets a value in each trial, either sampled or from a default.
- ✗ **D. Exact optima:** random search finds no exact optimum; it finds good values by sampling and a grid can contain good values too.

## Key idea
Random search tests many distinct values per hyperparameter, which beats a grid when only a few hyperparameters matter.
Q011455:
## Why ML assets move through stages
MLOps manages three kinds of assets: code, data and models. Early in development the assets change often and are not rigorously tested, so access can be wide. In the middle stage they are tested automatically. In production they are tightly controlled. Mixing these in one place means an experiment can break a production job or read data it should not.
## The recommended layout
Databricks recommends a separate **execution environment** per stage, with clearly defined transitions between them. An execution environment is the place where code creates or consumes models and data: compute instances, runtimes, libraries and automated jobs. The common names are development, staging and production. In Unity Catalog this is usually expressed as a `dev`, `staging` and `prod` catalog (three-level names such as `prod.ml.churn_features`), so privileges can differ per stage. Models created in development are registered to the `dev` catalog.
Note the legacy workspace model registry used fixed stages (Staging, Production) on one model; Unity Catalog models use catalogs for environments and aliases for roles such as Champion.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. One workspace with legacy stages:** moving versions between stage labels does not isolate compute, data or access, and registry stages belong to the legacy workspace registry rather than the Unity Catalog approach.
- ✓ **B. (correct):** Separate environments per stage, each with its own compute and a matching catalog, give each stage its own access control and clear promotion points. This is the layout the Databricks MLOps guidance describes.
- ✗ **C. Isolate only production:** development and staging have different purposes (free experiments versus automated, repeatable tests). Merging them removes the clean testing step that gates a release.
- ✗ **D. Prefixes in one catalog:** prefixes are only a naming convention. They give no separate privileges, compute or jobs, so a mistake in development can still touch production assets.

## Key idea
One environment per stage (dev, staging, prod), each with its own compute and catalog, and defined transitions between them.
Q011456:
## Deploy code or deploy models
There are two deployment patterns:
- **Deploy models**: train once in development and copy the model artifact to production.
- **Deploy code**: move the ML pipeline code (feature computation, training, validation, inference) from the development branch to staging and then the release branch, and let each environment run it.
## Which Databricks recommends
In most situations Databricks recommends deploying code. All code in the ML development process then goes through the same review and integration testing as any software, and the production model is trained on production code with access to production data. Deploying models can be right when training is very expensive or production data cannot be used for training in the target environment, but it is the exception.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Metrics only:** metrics are evidence, not a deployable asset. Manual re-training in production is not repeatable and bypasses version control and automated tests.
- ✗ **B. Promote data and generate code:** data is not the unit of promotion, and code created on the fly has no review or version history. Code belongs in Git.
- ✗ **C. Promote the artifact:** this is the "deploy models" pattern. It skips review of the training code and does not prove the model can be retrained in the target environment, so it is not the default recommendation.
- ✓ **D. (correct):** Code promotion makes every change pass code review and integration tests, and the production model is trained by production code, so the training process itself is what gets promoted.

## Key idea
Default MLOps pattern: promote code, not models, so production models are trained by reviewed and tested production code.
Q011457:
## Access control and versioning on Databricks
The MLOps guidance names four building blocks:
- **Git** for version control of pipelines and code. Databricks Git folders (formerly Repos) connect a Git provider to the workspace, so a stage change is a branch change (development branch, staging branch, release branch).
- **Delta tables in a lakehouse** for raw data and feature tables, with access controls that say who may read and modify them.
- **MLflow** to track parameters, metrics, artifacts and code snapshots during training.
- **Models in Unity Catalog** to manage model versions, governance and deployment status.
Anything that bypasses these (personal copies, direct production edits, unmanaged files) removes the history and access control that make the process auditable.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Unmanaged files:** the recommendation is Delta tables with access controls, not loose files in an arbitrary format.
- ✗ **B. Personal folders:** copied notebooks have no version control or review and are not tested before reaching production.
- ✗ **C. Write access to prod:** production assets should be tightly controlled. Data scientists typically get read-only access to production data, and changes go through pipelines.
- ✓ **D. MLflow plus Unity Catalog models (correct):** MLflow records how a model was produced, and Unity Catalog manages versions, governance and deployment status in one place.
- ✓ **E. Git and Git folders (correct):** code in Git gives review, history and a clear way to promote logic between stages.

## Key idea
Git for code, Delta tables for data and features, MLflow for tracking, Unity Catalog models for model lifecycle.
Q011458:
## Validation then deployment
After training, the model is registered to Unity Catalog in the catalog of the environment that ran the pipeline. A **model validation** task takes the model URI from the training task (passed with task values in a multitask job), loads the model, and runs checks. The checks depend on context: basic format and metadata checks, and for regulated industries compliance checks and performance on data slices.
If the checks pass, the model gets the **Challenger** alias. If they fail, the process ends and can notify users. A **model deployment** task then either promotes the Challenger directly by moving the **Champion** alias to the new version, or compares Challenger and Champion first. Aliases are named pointers to model versions, so promotion is an alias update, not a copy.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. (correct):** Passing validation earns the Challenger alias, which marks the version as a candidate for the deployment step and lets it be compared with the current Champion.
- ✗ **B. Legacy stage change:** stages belong to the legacy workspace registry and moving one does not itself serve traffic. Serving is configured separately by the deployment step.
- ✗ **C. Delete and re-register:** replacing versions destroys lineage and history. Versions are kept and an alias moves between them.
- ✗ **D. Regenerate AutoML notebook:** AutoML notebooks come from the exploration and baseline step and are not an approval mechanism.

## Key idea
Pass validation, get the Challenger alias; the deployment step then moves Champion by an alias update.
Q011459:
## Development data in the recommended layout
Ideally data scientists in the development workspace get read-only access to the prod catalog, including production data, inference tables and metric tables. That lets them analyze how production models perform and load production models to compare against new ones. Read-only is the key: they can look but cannot change production assets.
When policy blocks even that, the documented fallback is a **snapshot of production data written to the dev catalog**. The snapshot is a copy that lives in the environment where experimentation is allowed, so project code can be developed and evaluated on realistic data without touching production.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Weekend permissions:** a time window is still access to production assets, which is what the policy forbids.
- ✓ **B. (correct):** A snapshot in the dev catalog gives realistic data in the environment where data scientists have write access, without exposing the prod catalog.
- ✗ **C. Develop in production:** this removes the stage separation and shared accounts break audit trails.
- ✗ **D. Random data:** synthetic values rarely preserve distributions and correlations, so evaluation results would not predict real behavior.

## Key idea
No prod read access? Write a snapshot of production data to the dev catalog.
Q011460:
## Three stages, three goals
- **Development**: experimentation. Data scientists run EDA, build features and models, and the output is ML pipeline code.
- **Staging**: test the pipeline code to confirm it is ready for production. ML engineers build a CI pipeline that runs unit tests and integration tests against all ML pipeline code: model training, feature engineering pipelines, inference code and so on. The output is a **release branch** that triggers the CI/CD system to start the production stage.
- **Production**: tightly controlled execution of the released pipelines, model deployment and monitoring.
Staging is therefore about verifying code behaves correctly together, not about exploring data or serving users.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Backup of the production model:** model versions are kept in Unity Catalog with aliases; staging is not a backup location.
- ✗ **B. Interactive exploration:** that is the development stage's EDA step, which is not part of a deployed pipeline.
- ✓ **C. (correct):** Staging runs unit and integration tests over all pipeline code in CI, and its release branch is what triggers the production stage.
- ✗ **D. First user traffic:** serving users happens in production, after testing. Skipping tests to gather feedback reverses the order of the stages.

## Key idea
