Development experiments, staging tests all pipeline code in CI and cuts a release branch, production runs it under tight control.
Q011461:
## What Databricks Runtime ML is
Databricks Runtime for Machine Learning (Runtime ML) is a runtime version that automates the creation of compute with ML and deep learning infrastructure already installed: popular libraries for classical ML, deep learning and distributed training, in versions that are tested together.
## Top-tier libraries
Databricks designates a subset of libraries as **top-tier**. They get a faster update cadence (latest package releases with each runtime release, barring dependency conflicts) plus advanced support, testing and embedded integrations. You can still install extra libraries, either compute-scoped (for all notebooks on the compute) or notebook-scoped (only that session).

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Single-node engine:** Runtime ML still uses Spark and can run multi-node. It does not remove Spark.
- ✓ **B. (correct):** Runtime ML bundles pre-built and compatible ML libraries, so a new cluster is ready without manual dependency resolution, and top-tier libraries are kept current.
- ✗ **C. Automatic conversion:** a scikit-learn model stays a scikit-learn model. Conversion to Spark ML would be explicit code.
- ✗ **D. GPU without changes:** GPU use needs a GPU instance type, and the library must support GPUs. The runtime does not give code free GPU acceleration.

## Key idea
Runtime ML = ready, tested ML/DL libraries with a faster update cadence for top-tier ones.
Q011462:
## Access mode and the ML runtime
Compute has an **access mode**. To read Unity Catalog data on compute that runs Databricks Runtime ML, you must set the access mode to **Dedicated**. When you check the Machine learning box in the create-compute UI, Databricks sets this automatically, with you as the dedicated user. You can reassign a Dedicated resource to a user or a group; when assigned to a group, each member's permissions are scoped down to the group's permissions, so group members can share it securely.
Other modes are different: Standard (formerly shared) does not support AutoML, and no isolation shared does not support Unity Catalog.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. (correct):** Dedicated access mode is set automatically with the Machine learning option, and it is what allows Unity Catalog access on the ML runtime.
- ✗ **B. Standard:** Standard mode supports Unity Catalog but not AutoML, and it is not what the ML option selects.
- ✗ **C. No isolation shared:** this mode does not support Unity Catalog at all, so it could not read the tables under governance.
- ✗ **D. Serverless:** the question concerns classic compute with the ML runtime. Classic compute always has an access mode.

## Key idea
ML runtime + Unity Catalog = Dedicated access mode, set automatically by the Machine learning option.
Q011463:
## What Photon accelerates
Photon is a native vectorized engine. On Runtime ML (when enabled) it improves performance for Spark SQL, Spark DataFrames, feature engineering, GraphFrames and `xgboost4j` (the JVM XGBoost). It is not expected to help Spark RDDs, Pandas UDFs and non-JVM languages such as Python. So the Python XGBoost package, PyTorch and TensorFlow see no gain, and scikit-learn training is also Python.
Also, Spark RDD APIs and Spark MLlib have limited compatibility with Photon, and with large data they can hit Spark memory issues.
## Practical rule
Use Photon for the data-preparation steps, and look elsewhere (bigger or GPU instances, distributed libraries, parallel tuning) to speed up single-node Python training.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Dedicated mode disables Photon:** the ML compute default is Dedicated and Photon can be enabled on it. The Spark SQL speed-up proves it runs.
- ✗ **B. Outside Unity Catalog:** Photon works with Unity Catalog tables. The location of the data does not explain this.
- ✓ **C. (correct):** Photon is a SQL and DataFrame engine on the JVM side; scikit-learn and Python XGBoost training run in Python processes it does not touch, which matches the observed split.
- ✗ **D. Requires GPU:** Photon targets CPU query processing and does not depend on GPUs.

## Key idea
Photon speeds up Spark SQL/DataFrame work, not Python ML libraries such as scikit-learn, XGBoost or PyTorch.
Q011464:
## Custom environments on the ML runtime
Runtime ML ships with many libraries, but you can extend it:
- **Compute-scoped libraries**: installed on the compute resource, so they are available to every notebook on it. Use for a shared dependency.
- **Notebook-scoped libraries** (`%pip install ...`): visible only inside that notebook session. Use to try versions without affecting colleagues.
- **Init scripts** can install libraries when compute is created.
Caution: AutoML is stricter than normal notebooks. Its runs fail if existing preinstalled library versions are modified.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Driver only:** init scripts run on cluster nodes at creation, so they are a documented way to install libraries for the compute.
- ✗ **B. Blocked:** the docs say you can install additional libraries to create a custom environment.
- ✗ **C. Shared %pip:** notebook-scoped installs are per session; they do not leak to other notebooks, which is their advantage.
- ✓ **D. Notebook-scoped library (correct):** it exists only in that notebook's session and does not alter anyone else's environment.
- ✓ **E. Compute-scoped library (correct):** it is installed on the compute, so every notebook on it sees it.

## Key idea
Compute-scoped libraries are shared by all notebooks on the compute; notebook-scoped ones are per session.
Q011465:
## Where Runtime ML fits today
Runtime ML remains the standard classic-compute environment for classical ML (scikit-learn, XGBoost, LightGBM), Spark MLlib and general deep-learning libraries. But for GPU compute running custom deep learning, such as model fine-tuning or training, the docs recommend **AI Runtime** instead. AI Runtime is serverless GPU compute with simplified setup, faster provisioning and better performance, and there is migration guidance for classic GPU workloads.
The decision: classical tabular ML on classic compute with Runtime ML; custom deep learning on GPU leans toward AI Runtime.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Photon for PyTorch:** Photon does not improve Python libraries such as PyTorch, and CPU compute is no answer for GPU training.
- ✓ **B. (correct):** The docs recommend AI Runtime, serverless GPU compute for deep learning, over Runtime ML for GPU workloads such as fine-tuning.
- ✗ **C. Classic only:** the docs say the opposite, recommending AI Runtime for these workloads and describing migration from classic GPU compute.
- ✗ **D. AutoML:** AutoML trains classification, regression and forecasting models with classical algorithms and does not fine-tune deep networks.

## Key idea
Classical ML on Runtime ML; GPU deep learning and fine-tuning go to AI Runtime (serverless GPU).
Q011466:
## What AutoML does
AutoML is still a documented, supported feature (not deprecated). What changed: from Databricks Runtime 18.0 ML, AutoML is no longer a built-in library of the ML runtime, so the questions here assume a runtime version that includes it.
AutoML automates the search for the best algorithm and hyperparameter configuration. You supply the dataset and the problem type (classification, regression or forecasting). AutoML then:
- cleans and prepares the data,
- orchestrates distributed model training and hyperparameter tuning across multiple algorithms,
- finds the best model with open-source evaluation algorithms from scikit-learn, xgboost, LightGBM, Prophet and ARIMA,
- presents the results, with the source code notebook for each trial.
For classification the algorithms are decision trees, random forests, logistic regression, XGBoost and LightGBM. Because each trial is a run with metrics, you compare models on your chosen metric.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. (correct):** AutoML searches across several algorithms with hyperparameter tuning and ranks the trials, so model selection is automated, not a single predefined choice.
- ✗ **B. Single logistic regression:** logistic regression is just one of the candidate algorithms, and there is no coefficient-only report.
- ✗ **C. Copy the last model:** AutoML starts from your dataset and problem type, not from a previously registered model.
- ✗ **D. User picks one:** AutoML's value is that it also explores which algorithm fits, not only one algorithm's hyperparameters.

## Key idea
AutoML runs many algorithm and hyperparameter trials, evaluates them and surfaces the best one.
Q011467:
## Problem types in AutoML
AutoML offers **classification**, **regression** and **forecasting**. Forecasting is for time-series prediction, where order and seasonality matter. On classic compute, the forecasting algorithms are Prophet and Auto-ARIMA. Regression is for numeric targets without a time structure (decision trees, random forests, linear regression with SGD, XGBoost, LightGBM). AutoML has no clustering mode.
For forecasting you also supply the time column and a horizon, because training and validation data must be split by time rather than randomly.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Clustering:** AutoML does not offer clustering, and cluster means would not forecast a future date.
- ✗ **B. Regression:** regression ignores time order and uses algorithms without seasonality handling. Also, it is not limited to one algorithm.
- ✓ **C. (correct):** Forecasting fits ordered, seasonal data, and its candidate models (Prophet, Auto-ARIMA) are built for trend and seasonality.
- ✗ **D. Classification:** the target is numeric, and framing it as a class loses the time structure.

## Key idea
Time-ordered target with seasonality means a forecasting experiment (Prophet, Auto-ARIMA).
Q011468:
## Controlling the input columns
AutoML cleans and prepares data, but you can steer it. You can specify which columns AutoML uses for training; you cannot remove the prediction target, or the time column used to split the data. You can also choose how null values are imputed (by default AutoML picks a method by column type and content). If you pick a non-default imputation method, AutoML skips semantic type detection.
Dropping noise columns such as surrogate ids prevents the model from latching onto an identifier, which would generalize poorly to new customers.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Always every column:** the docs say you can specify which columns to use.
- ✗ **B. Delete the target:** with no label there is nothing to classify. The target is required.
- ✗ **C. Rename to "label":** names do not mark columns as ignored, and the target is selected explicitly.
- ✓ **D. (correct):** Column selection is a supported option, and the target and time-split columns are the ones you cannot remove.

## Key idea
Exclude unwanted columns in the AutoML configuration; the target and time-split columns must stay.
Q011469:
## AutoML and feature tables
In the classification, regression and forecasting setup you can choose **Use existing feature tables** to augment the original input dataset. AutoML joins the feature table(s) to your labeled input on the feature table's key, then runs its normal search on the enriched data. The input dataset still supplies the label.
This reuses curated, governed features instead of duplicating logic, and it helps AutoML find useful predictors that are not in the base table.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Replace the dataset:** the labeled dataset remains the base input. The feature table adds columns.
- ✓ **B. (correct):** Feature store integration augments the input dataset with columns from existing feature tables, so the churn model sees usage metrics without a manual export.
- ✗ **C. Manual CSV export:** not needed, since feature tables are directly supported as an augmentation source.
- ✗ **D. Register as a model:** a feature table is data, not a model, so registering it makes no sense.

## Key idea
AutoML can add features by joining existing feature tables to the labeled input dataset.
Q011470:
## Explainability in AutoML notebooks
Shapley values come from game theory and estimate how much each feature contributes to individual predictions, which makes them a common way to rank feature importance. The notebooks AutoML writes for regression and classification include SHAP code in a **Feature importance** section. The calculation is highly memory-intensive, so it does not run by default. To use it, set `shap_enabled = True` in that section and re-run the notebook, with enough memory on the compute.
This is an example of AutoML's glass-box style: model selection and importance analysis are visible code you can run and change.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Forecasting only:** the notebooks for regression and classification are the ones that include Shapley code.
- ✗ **B. Always computed:** the opposite is true, because the calculation is costly and off by default.
- ✓ **C. (correct):** The generated classification and regression notebooks contain SHAP code that is disabled by default for memory reasons, and turning it on is a one-line change.
- ✗ **D. Paid add-on:** SHAP is an open-source package used inside the notebook, not a separate product.

## Key idea
AutoML notebooks include SHAP, disabled by default; set shap_enabled = True to compute feature importance.
Q011471:
## Glass-box AutoML
Many "AutoML" tools return only a model, a black box. Databricks AutoML generates the **source code** for each trial as a Python notebook. For classification and regression the data exploration notebook and the best trial notebook are imported into your workspace. You can read the preprocessing steps, see the algorithm and hyperparameters, re-run it and edit it.
That makes AutoML useful beyond a quick baseline: it is a code generator that starts the project, and the team can take the notebook and build on it. For audits, the notebook is the record of how the model was built, and the trial is also logged in MLflow.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Hidden internals:** Databricks AutoML exposes the code instead of hiding it.
- ✗ **B. Compiled binary:** the output includes notebooks and MLflow runs with models, not a locked binary.
- ✗ **C. Auto-filing:** AutoML never contacts regulators or files documentation for you. The notebook is evidence the team can hand over itself.
- ✓ **D. (correct):** The generated notebook for the best trial is real, editable code, which allows review, reproduction and modification.

## Key idea
AutoML is glass box: each trial comes with editable source code you can audit and extend.
Q011472:
## What AutoML is good for
AutoML accelerates the early part of the lifecycle:
- It **cleans and prepares data** and builds baselines across algorithms, with a data exploration notebook that has summary statistics. Baselines tell you whether the data can solve the problem and set a bar to beat.
- Each trial is recorded in **MLflow** (parameters, metrics, artifacts, model), so you can sort runs, compare them and register one model.
- It generates trial notebooks, so you can start from working code.
It does not replace judgement: you still evaluate on held-out data, choose the business metric, and decide whether to deploy.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. MLflow tracking (correct):** every trial is an MLflow run, so comparison and registration are straightforward.
- ✗ **B. Guaranteed better:** no tool can promise this; AutoML is a baseline and starting point, and domain features can beat it.
- ✗ **C. Automatic deployment:** AutoML presents results. Registration and deployment are separate decisions, typically with validation first.
- ✗ **D. No held-out evaluation:** AutoML evaluates on validation and test splits, and you still check results against your requirements.
- ✓ **E. Baselines and exploration (correct):** AutoML builds baseline models quickly and summarizes the dataset, which shortens EDA.

## Key idea
AutoML gives fast baselines, an exploration notebook and MLflow-tracked trials to build on.
Q011473:
## Where generated notebooks live
For **classification and regression**, AutoML auto-imports into the workspace the data exploration notebook and the notebook for the best trial. Notebooks for other trials are saved as MLflow artifacts instead, not imported. For these trials `notebook_path` and `notebook_url` in the TrialInfo are not set. Open the MLflow run, find the IPython notebook under **Artifacts**, and download and import it if your admins allow artifact downloads.
For **forecasting**, notebooks for all trials are imported automatically.
The results of each experiment, including exploration and training notebooks, live in a `databricks_automl` folder in the home folder of the user who ran it.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. (correct):** Non-best trial notebooks are stored in each run's Artifacts, and you import them manually.
- ✗ **B. Best trial only:** all trials get code; only the best is auto-imported.
- ✗ **C. Driver disk:** artifacts are logged to MLflow storage and persist beyond the cluster.
- ✗ **D. Inside the model files:** the model is a separate artifact from the generated notebook.

## Key idea
Classification/regression: exploration and best-trial notebooks are imported; other trial notebooks are MLflow run artifacts.
Q011474:
## AutoML library requirements
AutoML relies on the `databricks-automl-runtime` package and on the library versions preinstalled in Runtime ML. The documented requirement is that **no additional libraries other than those preinstalled** should be installed on the cluster, and any modification (removal, upgrade or downgrade) to existing library versions makes runs fail because of incompatibility.
Fix: run AutoML on a clean Runtime ML cluster (or revert the change). Use a separate cluster, or notebook-scoped installs, for projects that need other versions.
Other requirements: a compute access mode that supports AutoML (Dedicated is supported, Standard is not) and open network ports to access workspace files.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. SHAP memory:** SHAP is disabled by default and is not required for a run.
- ✗ **B. Serverless only:** AutoML supports classic compute with Runtime ML.
- ✗ **C. Python 2 interpreter:** this is not a real requirement, because current runtimes use Python 3 and a pip upgrade of one library does not change the interpreter.
- ✓ **D. (correct):** Changing preinstalled library versions breaks the compatibility AutoML depends on, which fails the runs.

## Key idea
Do not change the preinstalled library versions on AutoML clusters; upgrades make runs fail.
Q011475:
## When AutoML pays off
AutoML shines on new, standard tabular problems (classification, regression, forecasting) where you need a strong baseline fast. It runs multiple algorithms in parallel with hyperparameter tuning, logs each trial in MLflow, and produces code you can build on.
It does not help where the work is custom or about judgement: a research architecture with a custom loss needs your own code; a dashboard aggregation is SQL; the choice of business metric and the cost of errors is a decision for people who understand the use case.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Custom research model:** AutoML uses a fixed list of algorithms, not custom architectures.
- ✗ **B. Metric and cost decision:** this is a business judgement that tools cannot make for you.
- ✓ **C. (correct):** AutoML saves the most time when you need a broad, tracked search over standard algorithms on a new dataset.
- ✗ **D. SQL aggregation:** no model is trained, so AutoML adds nothing.

## Key idea
AutoML = fast, broad, tracked baseline for standard tasks; custom models and business choices stay with you.
Q011476:
## Feature tables in Unity Catalog
In Unity Catalog, **any Delta table with a primary key constraint can serve as a feature table**. No special table type exists. You can create one with Databricks SQL, the Python `FeatureEngineeringClient` (package `databricks-feature-engineering`), or Lakeflow pipelines, then update, browse and govern it with Unity Catalog, using the three-level name `catalog.schema.table`.
The key matters because feature lookups join on it: at training and inference, features for an entity (a customer, a product) are fetched by primary key, with an optional timestamp key for time series.
## Feature Views and legacy name
For new projects Databricks now recommends **Feature Views**, which define features declaratively and let Databricks manage the pipelines. Feature tables, where you write the values yourself, remain fully supported and suit workloads that need Delta Sharing; both produce Unity Catalog-governed features.
Before Unity Catalog support, features lived in the **Workspace Feature Store**, a workspace-level feature table, now deprecated.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Catalog name suffix:** names carry no meaning to the feature store. The constraint does.
- ✓ **B. (correct):** A primary key constraint is the requirement; with it any Unity Catalog Delta table works as a feature table.
- ✗ **C. Liquid Clustering:** this is a layout optimization, unrelated to feature table status.
- ✗ **D. Model alias:** aliases apply to registered models, not to tables.

## Key idea
UC feature table = Delta table with a primary key.
Q011477:
## Workspace-scoped versus metastore-scoped
The legacy Workspace Feature Store keeps feature tables in a workspace, with workspace-level access control. Sharing across workspaces meant extra setup.
Feature tables in Unity Catalog are Delta tables registered in a metastore with a three-level name. A feature table in Unity Catalog is accessible to **all workspaces assigned to the table's metastore**, and access is governed by Unity Catalog privileges (for example `SELECT` to read, plus catalog and schema privileges) like any other data asset. Sharing outside the account is possible with Delta Sharing.
Tags, lineage and discovery in Catalog Explorer come along because the feature table is a standard Unity Catalog securable.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. (correct):** Metastore-level scope and Unity Catalog privileges let Team B use the same governed feature table without a copy.
- ✗ **B. Auto copy:** there is no copying, one table is shared by reference.
- ✗ **C. No access control:** Unity Catalog adds fine-grained privileges. Only users granted them can read or modify.
- ✗ **D. Creator workspace only:** opposite of the documented behavior.

## Key idea
UC feature tables: one governed copy, usable from every workspace on the metastore.
Q011478:
## Why move to Unity Catalog
Workspace-level feature tables (legacy Workspace Feature Store, deprecated and only available for workspaces created before August 19, 2024) have their own governance. Unity Catalog feature tables use the same governance layer as all other data:
- **Access control** with Unity Catalog privileges and the three-level namespace; tags for categorizing tables and features.
- **Lineage**: when you train and log a model using Feature Engineering in Unity Catalog, the tables and functions used are tracked and shown in Catalog Explorer.
- **Sharing** across workspaces on the same metastore.
Feature tables are still Delta tables with a primary key, and you own the pipeline that populates them.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Auto recompute:** you write and refresh the data with your own pipeline; feature tables are not recomputed per query.
- ✗ **B. Proprietary format:** feature tables are standard Delta tables.
- ✓ **C. Unity Catalog privileges (correct):** feature tables are securable objects, so the same grants and audit as other tables apply.
- ✗ **D. No key needed:** the primary key is required and is the join key for lookups.
- ✓ **E. Lineage (correct):** models log which feature tables and functions built them, and Catalog Explorer displays it.

## Key idea
UC feature tables bring UC governance, lineage and metastore-wide sharing.
Q011479:
## Reusing an existing Delta table
You do not have to duplicate data. A Delta table in Unity Catalog that has a primary key constraint can serve as a feature table. If the table lacks a primary key, use `ALTER TABLE` DDL to add the constraint, for example:
`ALTER TABLE ml.crm.customer_attrs ADD CONSTRAINT customer_pk PRIMARY KEY (customer_id)`
After that the table can be used in training sets through the Feature Engineering client. Streaming tables and materialized views from Lakeflow pipelines need the key in their definition instead, followed by a refresh.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Export to legacy store:** the legacy store is deprecated and unrelated to a Unity Catalog table.
- ✓ **B. (correct):** Adding the primary key constraint turns the existing governed table into a feature table without a copy.
- ✗ **C. Recreate in a special catalog:** any catalog and schema is fine, and copying duplicates data.
- ✗ **D. Materialized view:** materialized views are not required, and a view is not what makes lookups possible.

## Key idea
Existing UC Delta table + primary key constraint = feature table, no copy.
Q011480:
## Feature governance and lineage
When you train and log a model with a training set built from Unity Catalog feature tables, Databricks stores the feature specification with the model and tracks **lineage** across the feature tables, functions and models. In Catalog Explorer you can open a feature table and see the models (and notebooks and jobs) that use it, which is the impact analysis needed before changing a column.
The legacy Workspace Feature Store had lineage as well, but at workspace level. In Unity Catalog the lineage sits with the other governance metadata.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Alias:** an alias is a pointer to a model version and does not store training tables.
- ✗ **B. Cluster event log:** it records cluster events like start and resize, not table-level lineage.
- ✗ **C. AutoML exploration notebook:** it summarizes the input dataset and does not track downstream consumers.
- ✓ **D. (correct):** Feature lineage links feature tables to downstream models, so you can list the models affected by a change.

## Key idea
UC feature tables plus models trained from them give lineage you can inspect before changing a table.
Q011481:
## Finding runs programmatically
Every MLflow run records its parameters and metrics on the tracking server that Databricks hosts. To analyze them in code you query the experiment instead of opening runs one by one. The MLflow Python `mlflow.search_runs` function returns a pandas DataFrame with one row per run; the Spark data source for experiments returns a Spark DataFrame instead.
## The arguments that matter
- `experiment_ids` limits the search to one or more experiments (note that `1234` here is an experiment ID, not a run ID).
- `filter_string` keeps only matching runs, for example `metrics.rmse < 1.0`.
- `order_by` sorts runs by a key with `ASC` or `DESC`, for example `metrics.rmse ASC`.
- `max_results` caps the number of rows returned.
Sorting by the metric in the direction where "better" comes first and keeping one row is the standard way to get the best run. For an error metric such as RMSE, smaller is better, so the order is ascending.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Descending order:** `DESC` puts the largest RMSE first, so this returns the worst run of the 60, not the best.
- ✗ **B. `mlflow.get_run`:** it takes a run ID, not an experiment ID, and returns one run object. It cannot rank 60 runs, and sorting the metrics of a single run says nothing about the other trials.
- ✓ **C. (correct):** Sorting ascending by `metrics.rmse` puts the smallest error first, and `max_results=1` keeps only that row, so the DataFrame holds exactly the best run.
- ✗ **D. MIN in the filter:** `filter_string` compares a metric with a literal number; it has no aggregate such as `MIN` to pick the lowest value among runs. Ranking is done with `order_by`.

## Key idea
Best run = `search_runs` ordered by the metric (ASC for error, DESC for score) with `max_results=1`.
Q011482:
## Two entry points for the same query
MLflow offers the search in two forms. The fluent function `mlflow.search_runs` returns a pandas DataFrame, which is convenient for analysis in a notebook. The `MlflowClient().search_runs` method of the Client API returns a list of `Run` objects (with `run.info.run_id`, `run.data.metrics`, `run.data.params`), which is convenient when you only need IDs and values to pass on to the next step, such as model registration.
Both accept `order_by` and `max_results`, so "best run" is the same recipe with either: order by the metric in the better direction and keep one result.
## What is not available
There is no "best run" property on an experiment, and the search does not rank by a metric unless you ask it to with `order_by`.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Experiment `best_run`:** the experiment object has no such attribute. MLflow does not pick a winner on its own; you query for it.
- ✗ **B. Last active run:** `mlflow.last_active_run()` returns the most recently active run of the current process. Recency has nothing to do with the metric, so it may well be a poor trial.
- ✗ **C. No `order_by`:** nothing in the call names `val_accuracy`, so no ranking by that metric happens and the first row is just whichever run comes first, not the most accurate.
- ✓ **D. DataFrame search (correct):** ordering by `metrics.val_accuracy DESC` puts the highest accuracy first and `max_results=1` keeps it, giving a one-row pandas DataFrame.
- ✓ **E. Client API search (correct):** `MlflowClient().search_runs` takes the same `order_by` and `max_results`, so the first element of the returned list is the run with the highest accuracy.

## Key idea
MLflow never ranks runs for you: use `order_by` on the metric plus `max_results=1`, with `mlflow.search_runs` (DataFrame) or `MlflowClient().search_runs` (list of Run objects).
Q011483:
## Which object do you hold?
The return type decides the syntax, and the two search APIs differ.
- `mlflow.search_runs` returns a pandas DataFrame. Each run is a row, with a `run_id` column and one column per logged value named `metrics.<name>`, `params.<name>` and `tags.<name>`.
- `MlflowClient().search_runs` returns a list of `Run` objects, read with attribute access such as `run.info.run_id` and `run.data.params["max_depth"]`.
Parameters are stored as strings, so the `params.max_depth` cell holds text such as `"8"` and needs a cast (`int(...)`) before it is used as a number.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. (correct):** The call returns a DataFrame, so the run ID is the `run_id` column and the hyperparameter sits in the column `params.max_depth`, both read from row 0.
- ✗ **B. Missing prefix:** the column is called `params.max_depth`, not `max_depth`, and `best["run_id"]` returns a whole column (a Series), not the single value.
- ✗ **C. Attribute access on the DataFrame:** a DataFrame has no `info` or `data` attributes. Those belong to `Run` objects returned by the Client API.
- ✗ **D. List-of-Run syntax:** indexing `best[0]` and reading `.info` / `.data` works for the Client API, which returns Run objects. On a DataFrame, `best[0]` looks for a column named 0 and raises a KeyError.

## Key idea
`mlflow.search_runs` gives a DataFrame (columns `run_id`, `metrics.x`, `params.x`); `MlflowClient().search_runs` gives Run objects (`run.info`, `run.data`).
Q011484:
## Run search syntax
`filter_string` uses a small SQL-like grammar over the data stored in a run. Because metrics, parameters, tags and run attributes live in different namespaces, each key must say which one it comes from.
- `metrics.rmse < 1.0` compares a logged metric with a number.
- `tags.team = 'fraud'` compares a tag with a string (string values are quoted).
- `attributes.status = 'FINISHED'` or the short form `attribute.status` filters on run attributes.
- Conditions are joined with `AND`; there is no `WHERE` keyword and no dictionary form.
The same expressions work in the search field of the experiment page in the Databricks UI, for example `metrics.r2 > 0.3`.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Dictionary filter:** `filter_string` is a string. There is no dictionary form for the comparison operators.
- ✓ **B. (correct):** A bare name such as `rmse` is not a valid identifier in the grammar. With the `metrics.` and `tags.` prefixes the expression parses and filters correctly.
- ✗ **C. Using `order_by`:** `order_by` only sorts. Metrics can be filtered, so moving the condition would also drop the `team` condition and the threshold would no longer apply.
- ✗ **D. `WHERE` keyword:** the filter string is only the condition, so adding `WHERE` itself causes another parse error.

## Key idea
In run searches name the namespace: `metrics.`, `params.`, `tags.`; combine with `AND`; no `WHERE`.
Q011485:
## Metrics are time series, parameters are not
`mlflow.log_metric("val_loss", value, step=epoch)` can be called many times with the same key. MLflow stores every value with its step, so a metric is a series, and the run page draws it as a chart.
- In the experiment search field, a plain metric condition such as `metrics.val_loss <= 0.2` is checked against the last logged value of the metric.
- `MIN(metrics.val_loss) <= 0.2` and `MAX(metrics.x) > 0.9` check the lowest or highest value in the metric history instead. Only runs logged after August 2024 have these minimum and maximum values.
- `LATEST(metrics.x)` states the default explicitly.
- Parameters are logged once per run and hold configuration such as `max_depth`, not training curves.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. `LOWEST`:** the documented aggregates are `MIN`, `MAX` and `LATEST`; `LOWEST` is not part of the grammar.
- ✓ **B. (correct):** `MIN(metrics.val_loss) <= 0.2` looks at the whole history of the metric, so it keeps every run whose loss reached 0.2 at any epoch.
- ✗ **C. Plain metric condition:** it is evaluated against the last logged value, so a run whose loss dipped to 0.2 and rose again is missed.
- ✗ **D. `params.`:** parameters are single configuration values written once; a metric is stored in the metric store, so a parameter filter on `val_loss` finds nothing.

## Key idea
UI metric filters use the last value; wrap the key in `MIN(...)` or `MAX(...)` to test the history.
Q011486:
## Autolog and manual logging together
Autologging patches supported libraries (scikit-learn, Spark ML, XGBoost, TensorFlow and others) so that `fit` records parameters, metrics and the model with no extra code. It is the quickest way to start tracking.
Manual logging gives control over what is recorded. The calls work on the active run and can be mixed with autologging:
- `mlflow.log_param` / `mlflow.log_params` for configuration values
- `mlflow.log_metric` / `mlflow.log_metrics` for numbers, optionally with `step`
- `mlflow.log_artifact`, `mlflow.log_figure`, `mlflow.log_dict`, `mlflow.log_text` for files and plots
- `mlflow.set_tag` for searchable labels
A common pattern is autolog for the standard training information plus a few manual calls for domain metrics and custom plots.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. (correct):** Manual calls attach to the run that autologging opened (or to one you start with `mlflow.start_run()`), so the plot and the custom metric appear next to the automatically logged values.
- ✗ **B. Delta table:** you can store results in a table, but then they are not attached to the run. MLflow accepts arbitrary metrics and artifacts through its logging API.
- ✗ **C. Disabling autologging:** nothing in MLflow makes the two approaches exclusive. Dropping autologging would only add work.
- ✗ **D. Hyperparameters trick:** only estimator parameters are logged as parameters, and a metric belongs in the metric store where it can be sorted and charted. A plot cannot be stored as a parameter at all.

## Key idea
Autolog for the defaults, manual `log_metric` / `log_figure` / `log_artifact` calls for anything else, in the same run.
Q011487:
## Parameters versus metrics
MLflow separates two kinds of key-value data on a run.
- **Parameters** describe the configuration of the run: hyperparameters, dataset version, feature list. They are written once, stored as strings and cannot be overwritten with a different value in the same run. They are used to filter and group runs.
- **Metrics** describe results: loss, accuracy, RMSE. They are numeric and can be logged many times with the same key. Each call adds a point with a `step` (and timestamp), so the run keeps a history that the UI plots as a chart.
Because the optimizer's changing learning rate is not reported to MLflow unless you log it, a value that changes over time belongs in a metric, with a step, rather than a parameter.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Overwrite behavior:** metrics append rather than replace. The run page and the history API show every logged step, while `run.data.metrics` shows only the latest one.
- ✗ **B. Automatic update:** MLflow records only what you log; it does not observe the optimizer, and parameters are not time series.
- ✗ **C. String metrics:** metrics are numbers. That is what lets the search compare them with `<`, `>` and sort by them.
- ✓ **D. Metric history (correct):** repeated `log_metric` calls with `step` append points, so all 20 loss values remain available for charts and `get_metric_history`.
- ✓ **E. Immutable string parameter (correct):** a parameter is saved as text, and MLflow rejects a second `log_param` with a different value for the same key in the same run.

## Key idea
Parameters are write-once strings for configuration; metrics are numeric and can be logged repeatedly with a step to form a history.
Q011488:
## A file versus an MLflow Model
`mlflow.log_artifact` copies any local file into the run's artifact location. MLflow treats it as an opaque file: it does not know what is inside.
`mlflow.<flavor>.log_model` writes a directory in the MLflow Model format:
- an `MLmodel` file that lists the flavors (for example `sklearn` and the generic `python_function`) and the model signature
- the serialized model
- `requirements.txt` and `conda.yaml` so the environment can be rebuilt
- an input example when you pass one
With this structure, `mlflow.pyfunc.load_model`, batch inference with a Spark UDF, registration with `mlflow.register_model` and Model Serving all work without custom code. A bare pickle supports none of them.
In MLflow 3 the call uses `name=` for the logged model (MLflow 2 called this argument `artifact_path`).

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Size limit:** there is no small size cap on `log_artifact` that `log_model` avoids; both write to the same artifact storage for the run.
- ✗ **B. Automatic Unity Catalog storage:** `log_artifact` does not register anything in Unity Catalog. Registration requires `register_model` or `registered_model_name` for a logged model.
- ✓ **C. (correct):** Logging the model with its flavor, signature and dependency files is what makes it loadable with one call, registrable in Unity Catalog and deployable on Model Serving.
- ✗ **D. Storage location:** both use the experiment's artifact location (MLflow-managed storage by default, or a Unity Catalog volume you choose). Neither writes to a different place by default.

## Key idea
Use `log_model` (flavor, signature, requirements) for models; use `log_artifact` for plain files such as reports and CSVs.
Q011489:
## Same data, four different places
A run holds several kinds of information, and each logging call writes to one of them.
- Parameters go to the parameter table (`log_param`, `log_params` for a dict).
- Metrics go to the metric table (`log_metric`, `log_metrics` for a dict of numbers).
- Tags are free labels (`set_tag`, `set_tags`), meant for metadata such as owner or data source.
- Artifacts are files (`log_artifact`, `log_artifacts` for a local directory, `log_dict` for a JSON/YAML file generated from a dict).
Only parameters and metrics can be compared across runs in the experiment table, sorted, and used in `metrics.rmse < 0.5` style filters. If the values land in an artifact or a tag, those features do not see them as metrics.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. `log_dict`:** it stores each dictionary as a JSON file in the artifacts. The values are not parameters or metrics, so they do not appear as columns in the runs table.
- ✗ **B. `log_artifacts`:** it expects a path to a local directory, not a dictionary, and it would copy files rather than record values.
- ✓ **C. (correct):** `log_params` writes a dictionary of hyperparameters in one call and `log_metrics` does the same for numeric results, so both land in the tables the experiment page compares and filters on.
- ✗ **D. `set_tags`:** tags are metadata labels stored as strings. Numeric results saved as tags cannot be charted or ordered as metrics.

## Key idea
Dict of hyperparameters -> `log_params`; dict of numbers -> `log_metrics`; `log_dict` and `log_artifacts` store files.
Q011490:
## One active run per thread
The fluent API keeps one active run at a time. Calling `mlflow.start_run()` while a run is active raises an exception, because MLflow cannot tell which run later `log_metric` calls belong to.
For tuning loops, where an outer "search" run groups many trial runs, MLflow supports nested runs: `mlflow.start_run(nested=True)` creates a child that records the parent run ID in a tag. The experiment page shows the children under the parent, and each child has its own parameters, metrics and artifacts. The parent can log the summary of the whole search.
Some tuning libraries do this for you: autologging and Hyperopt/`Trials` integrations create child runs per trial.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. (correct):** With `nested=True` the call is allowed even though a run is active, and the new run is linked as a child, so each trial is separately tracked and grouped under the outer run.
- ✗ **B. Ending the outer run:** this closes the parent so nothing groups the trials, and any later parent-level logging would silently create yet another run. The goal was a parent-child structure.
- ✗ **C. Run names:** a name is just a label. It does not lift the one-active-run rule, so the error remains.
- ✗ **D. Changing the experiment:** the active run is still open and `start_run` still raises. Moving trials to other experiments would also scatter them instead of grouping.

## Key idea
Need runs inside an active run (tuning trials) -> `mlflow.start_run(nested=True)`.
Q011491:
## What the run page records
A run page is the UI view of one run's tracking data. It shows:
- the run ID and details such as status, start time, duration and user
- the parameters and metrics saved with the run, with charts for metrics logged over steps
- tags
- a link to the source: the notebook version (a snapshot, shown with a highlight at the time of the run) that started the run
- the Artifacts tab, where plots, files and logged models appear. For a logged model the tab also shows code snippets to load it and predict on Spark and pandas DataFrames.
Since the notebook version is stored with the run, a result can be traced to the code that produced it even if the notebook was edited later.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Metrics as base64:** metrics are numbers shown in a table and charts; plots are files in the artifacts.
- ✓ **B. Artifacts tab (correct):** lists the files logged with `log_figure` or `log_artifact`, so the saved plots and the model are visible there.
- ✗ **C. Spark UI link:** the run page does not hold the query plans. Spark execution details live in the Spark UI of the cluster, not in the tracking record.
- ✗ **D. Permissions button:** it controls who may view or edit the run, but it is not an access log and lists no past viewers.
- ✓ **E. Source link (correct):** opens the notebook as it was when the run executed, so the exact code is known.

## Key idea
The run page shows parameters, metrics, tags, a link to the source notebook version, and artifacts including logged models.
Q011492:
## Filtering runs in the UI
The search field of the experiment details page accepts the same expression grammar as `search_runs`. Keys are prefixed with the data kind:
- `metrics.r2 > 0.3`
- `params.elasticNetParam = 0.5`
- `tags.estimator_name="RandomForestRegressor"` (string values in quotes)
- `MIN(metrics.rmse) <= 1` or `MAX(metrics.memUsage) > 0.9` to filter by the minimum or maximum of a metric history; by default a metric condition uses the last logged value.
Conditions are combined with `AND`. Tag keys with spaces are wrapped in backticks. State, creation time and datasets are chosen from drop-downs next to the search field.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. `params.` for everything:** R2 is a result, so it is logged as a metric, and the estimator name was stored as a tag. Parameter filters would look in the wrong table and find nothing.
- ✗ **B. SQL query:** the field is not a SQL console. It does not accept `SELECT ... FROM runs`.
- ✗ **C. Free text:** the field expects comparisons on prefixed keys; a loose list of words is not a valid expression.
- ✓ **D. (correct):** A metric is addressed as `metrics.r2` and a tag as `tags.estimator_name`, joined by `AND`, which is the documented expression form.

## Key idea
UI search = `metrics.`, `params.`, `tags.` prefixes joined with `AND`; `MIN(...)`/`MAX(...)` use the metric history.
Q011493:
## Notebook and workspace experiments
An experiment is the collection of runs that you compare. Databricks has two kinds.
- A **notebook experiment** exists for one notebook. If no experiment is active when `mlflow.start_run()` is called in a notebook, Databricks creates it automatically (it shares the notebook's name and ID), and runs from that notebook go there.
- A **workspace experiment** is not tied to a notebook. Any notebook, job or API call can log to it by name or ID, for example with `mlflow.set_experiment("/Shared/name_of_experiment")`.
So, to share one experiment between several authors, use a workspace experiment in a shared location and set it explicitly. The permissions on the experiment decide who can see and edit runs.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Merging notebooks:** any notebook can log to a workspace experiment, so merging only removes the independence of the three scientists.
- ✗ **B. Exporting and re-importing:** this is manual, creates duplicate runs without the original lineage and is unnecessary because runs can be logged to the shared experiment directly.
- ✗ **C. Default grouping:** each notebook's default is its own notebook experiment. Databricks does not merge notebooks by folder.
- ✓ **D. (correct):** A shared workspace experiment is the supported way to collect runs from several notebooks; each notebook only needs `set_experiment` with the same path.

## Key idea
One notebook -> notebook experiment by default; a team that wants one comparison view -> a workspace experiment set with `mlflow.set_experiment`.
Q011494:
## Soft delete of runs
Deleting runs from an experiment page is a soft delete. The runs leave the default (Active) list but are kept for 30 days.
- To see them, change the State filter on the experiment details page to Deleted.
- Select the runs and choose Restore to bring them back to the Active list.
- In Python, `mlflow.delete_runs` deletes runs created before a timestamp in bulk (Databricks Runtime 14.1 or later), and `mlflow.restore_runs` restores runs deleted after a timestamp.
If an experiment keeps hitting the quota on the number of runs, deleting runs that are no longer needed is the recommended action.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. (correct):** Within the 30-day window the runs can be listed with the Deleted state and restored, with their parameters, metrics and artifacts intact.
- ✗ **B. Trash folder:** runs deleted from an experiment page stay in that experiment with the Deleted state; they are recovered with the State filter, not from the workspace browser.
- ✗ **C. Only names kept:** the whole run record is kept during the retention period, not just names and parameters.
- ✗ **D. Permanent deletion:** a UI delete does not purge the run immediately, so recovery is possible for 30 days.

## Key idea
Deleted runs are kept for 30 days; filter State = Deleted and Restore to recover them.
Q011495:
## Where artifacts live
Parameters, metrics and tags are stored by the tracking server. Artifacts (plots, files, models) are written to the experiment's artifact location.
- Default: MLflow-managed storage `dbfs:/databricks/mlflow-tracking/<experiment-id>`.
- Recommended for Unity Catalog workspaces: a Unity Catalog volume path such as `dbfs:/Volumes/catalog/schema/volume/path`, set when the experiment is created.
- Other locations, for example a direct `s3://` URI, are possible but not recommended; their artifacts do not appear in the MLflow UI and models stored there cannot be registered in the Model Registry.
So a run can look healthy (metrics visible) while the artifact view is empty.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. No artifacts in workspace experiments:** workspace experiments store artifacts as any experiment does; the limitation is about the location.
- ✗ **B. Metastore admin sharing:** artifact visibility does not depend on membership of an admin group. It depends on the artifact location type and the permissions to read it.
- ✓ **C. (correct):** An S3 artifact location is outside the two supported UI locations, so the Artifacts tab cannot show the files and the model cannot be registered from there.

Q011497:

Q011498:
## Privileges to create a registered model
Models in Unity Catalog follow the usual Unity Catalog privilege model, in which privileges are granted on securable objects and checked down the hierarchy.
To create a new registered model you need:
- `USE CATALOG` on the enclosing catalog
- `USE SCHEMA` on the enclosing schema
- `CREATE MODEL` (or `CREATE FUNCTION`) on the schema, for example `GRANT CREATE MODEL ON SCHEMA prod.ml_team TO ds_team`
To add a new version to an existing registered model you must be its owner, or hold `CREATE MODEL VERSION` on it plus the `USE` privileges. To load a model for inference you need `EXECUTE` on the model.

- ✓ **A. CREATE MODEL (correct):** this is the privilege that allows creating a registered model object in the schema.
- ✗ **B. CREATE TABLE:** it allows creating tables, and a model is a separate securable type with its own privilege.
- ✗ **C. MODIFY on the metastore:** no metastore-wide write privilege is needed; privileges are scoped to the catalog, schema and model.
- ✗ **D. EXECUTE on the catalog:** `EXECUTE` is the privilege for loading or using a model and is held on the model, not required for creating one.
- ✓ **E. USE SCHEMA (correct):** privileges on objects in a schema are effective only when the user can also reach the schema, so `USE SCHEMA` is required together with `USE CATALOG`.

Create a UC model = `USE CATALOG` + `USE SCHEMA` + `CREATE MODEL`; loading it needs `EXECUTE`.
Q011499:
## Signatures are required in Unity Catalog

- pass an `input_example` to `mlflow.<flavor>.log_model`, and MLflow infers the signature from the example and the model's prediction (MLflow 2.5.0 or later)
- pass an explicit `signature` (for example from `mlflow.models.infer_signature`)
- use Databricks autologging, which logs models with signatures for many frameworks

- ✗ **B. Plain artifact:** a pickle logged as an artifact is not an MLflow Model and cannot be registered as a model version.
- ✓ **C. (correct):** An input example lets MLflow infer the signature when logging, which satisfies the requirement and keeps the model usable for serving and validation.
- ✗ **D. Disabling the check:** the signature requirement is not an optional setting an administrator can switch off; it must be supplied with the model version.

UC model versions need a signature: log with `input_example` or `signature`, or use autologging.
Q011500:
## Register at log time or after comparing

- **At log time**: pass `registered_model_name="cat.schema.model"` to `log_model`. Every call creates a new version, which is right when each run should be a candidate version.
- **After comparison**: log all candidates without a name, find the best one with `search_runs`, then call `mlflow.register_model(model_uri, name)` for that model only. This keeps the registry free of rejected versions.
What the URI looks like depends on the MLflow generation. In MLflow 3 a model is its own `LoggedModel` entity and is addressed as `models:/<model_id>` (it also records the parameters and metrics of its run). In MLflow 2 the URI points into the run's artifacts: `runs:/<run_id>/<artifact_path>`. Both go into the same `register_model(uri, name)` call.

- ✗ **A. Experiment ID in the URI:** the `runs:/` form needs a run ID plus the artifact path, not an experiment ID.
- ✗ **B. `create_registered_model`:** it creates an empty registered model from a name. It takes no model URI and creates no version.
- ✗ **C. Register-all-then-delete:** this works only in a technical sense; it pollutes version numbering and lineage with rejected candidates, and needs extra privileges to clean up.
- ✓ **D. (correct):** Registering after the comparison with the winner's model URI creates the registered model (or a new version of it) for that model only.

Compare first, then `mlflow.register_model(winner_uri, "cat.schema.model")`; MLflow 3 URIs are `models:/<model_id>`, MLflow 2 URIs are `runs:/<run_id>/<path>`.
Q011501:
## Workspace scope versus metastore scope

**Models in Unity Catalog** are objects in the metastore, so every workspace attached to that metastore sees the same registered models, subject to Unity Catalog privileges. Docs give exactly this example: models in the `prod` catalog can be used from a dev workspace to compare a new model with the production baseline.
Other benefits that come from the Unity Catalog integration are centralized access control, auditing, lineage back to the training data and model discovery across workspaces.

- ✗ **A. Export and import:** that is the workaround of a workspace-scoped registry. Models in Unity Catalog need no copies.
- ✗ **B. Registering in prod first:** the registry is not bound to the training workspace. Any workspace on the metastore can register to a catalog it has privileges on.
- ✓ **C. (correct):** Unity Catalog models are metastore-level objects, so a user with `USE CATALOG`, `USE SCHEMA` and `EXECUTE` can load the prod model from any workspace attached to the metastore.
- ✗ **D. Cluster policy:** access to a model is decided by Unity Catalog privileges, not by compute policies.

## Key idea
UC registry = metastore-wide, shared by all attached workspaces and governed by grants; the legacy workspace registry is private to one workspace.
Q011502:
## What Models in Unity Catalog add
Databricks documents Models in Unity Catalog as the recommended way to govern and deploy models. It extends Unity Catalog benefits to ML models:
- **Centralized access control**: privileges such as `EXECUTE` (use the model), `CREATE MODEL VERSION` and ownership are granted to users, groups or service principals.
- **Auditing**: access to securable objects is recorded in audit logs.
- **Lineage**: when a model is trained on Unity Catalog tables, logging the input with `mlflow.log_input` (or using feature engineering APIs) records the table-to-model lineage.
- **Discovery**: models appear in Catalog Explorer alongside tables, across workspaces.
Stages in the legacy workspace registry (Staging, Production, Archived) describe lifecycle position, not permissions.

- ✗ **A. Workspace registry stages:** a stage is a lifecycle label. It does not state who may load the model and does not trace data lineage.
- ✗ **B. Delta table of models:** a table would not be a model registry (no versions, signatures or loading by URI), and lineage and auditing exist for models themselves in Unity Catalog.
- ✗ **C. Git folder:** Git tracks code changes, not read access to a model or its training lineage, and it does not provide a governed serving source.
- ✓ **D. (correct):** Unity Catalog gives group-based privileges on the model, audit logs of access and lineage to the training tables, which covers all three audit needs in one system.

## Key idea
Governance needs (group grants, audit, lineage, discovery) -> Models in Unity Catalog.
Q011503:
## Two registries, two addressing schemes

Workspace registry = plain names + stages, one workspace; Unity Catalog = `catalog.schema.model` + aliases/versions, whole metastore.

Q011506:
## Counting fits
A parameter grid is the Cartesian product of the value lists, so 3 values of `regParam` and 4 values of `maxIter` give 3 x 4 = 12 `ParamMap`s (combinations). This arithmetic is a generally accepted definition, and the Spark ML tuning guide describes the same procedure.
- `CrossValidator` splits the data into `numFolds` pairs of training and validation sets and evaluates every `ParamMap` on every pair.
- Search fits = combinations x folds = 12 x 5 = 60.
- After the best `ParamMap` is chosen, `CrossValidator` re-fits the estimator on the entire dataset, which is one more fit (61 in total).

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. 61:** it adds the final refit on the full dataset, which the question explicitly leaves out.
- ✗ **B. 20:** it multiplies folds by only one parameter's values and ignores the other parameter, so it does not match the product of the grid.
- ✗ **C. 12:** this counts combinations only and forgets that every combination is repeated in each of the five folds.
- ✓ **D. 60 fits (correct):** each of the 12 combinations is trained once per fold, and the question excludes the refit.

## Key idea
Fits in a search = grid combinations x folds; the refit adds one more.
Q011507:
## Single split versus folds
The Spark ML tuning guide states that `TrainValidationSplit` evaluates each parameter combination once, in contrast to k times for `CrossValidator`. It creates one (training, validation) pair, for example 75% and 25% with `trainRatio=0.75`.
- Combinations: 3 x 2 = 6, so 6 fits during the search.
- Like `CrossValidator`, it finally fits the estimator with the best `ParamMap` on the entire dataset: 1 more fit.
- Total: 6 + 1 = 7.
The arithmetic is a generally accepted counting definition.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. 3 models:** it counts only one parameter's values, but a grid tries every combination of both parameters.
- ✓ **B. 7 models (correct):** six combinations are each fitted once on the training part, and the best one is refitted on the whole dataset.
- ✗ **C. 6 models:** this is correct for the search alone, but the question counts the final model trained on the whole dataset too.
- ✗ **D. 12 models:** a fit happens only on the training part; the validation part is used to score the model, so it never doubles the number of fits.

## Key idea
TrainValidationSplit = combinations fits + 1 refit; CrossValidator = combinations x folds + 1.
Q011508:
## Both factors grow
The number of fits is combinations x folds. The earlier setup gave 4 x 3 x 3 = 36 fits. Changing both the grid and the folds multiplies the effect:
- New combinations: 4 x 5 = 20.
- New fits: 20 x 5 = 100.
Cost grows roughly 2.8 times for a change that sounds small. With Spark ML you can set `parallelism` on the `CrossValidator` to evaluate several `ParamMap`s at once, but the count of fits stays the same.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. 100 fits (correct):** the new grid has 4 x 5 = 20 combinations, and each of them is trained once in each of the five folds.
- ✗ **B. 20:** it counts the combinations once and ignores that cross-validation repeats each combination in every fold.
- ✗ **C. 36:** it is the old configuration before the grid and the number of folds were changed.
- ✗ **D. 60:** it uses the five folds but keeps the old grid of 3 values for `minInstancesPerNode`.

## Key idea
Grid size and fold count multiply; widening both changes cost quickly.
Q011509:
## Where the count comes from
4 x 4 x 4 = 64 combinations, times 5 folds = 320 fits. Only changes to the grid size or to the number of evaluations per combination change this number. These counts are generally accepted arithmetic.
- `TrainValidationSplit` evaluates each combination once: 64 fits.
- 3 values per parameter and 3 folds: 27 x 3 = 81 fits.
- `parallelism` (in Spark ML, the number of `ParamMap`s evaluated at the same time) shortens wall-clock time but not the count.
- `collectSubModels` keeps the fitted sub-models for later inspection, which adds memory use and not fewer fits.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. collectSubModels:** it only stores the fitted models, so the number of fits stays at 320 and memory use grows.
- ✗ **B. Higher parallelism:** it runs up to eight evaluations concurrently, but the 320 fits still happen.
- ✗ **C. Second evaluator metric:** it changes how models are scored, not how many are fitted, so the count stays at 320.
- ✓ **D. TrainValidationSplit (correct):** one validation pair per combination, so 64 fits, below 100.
- ✓ **E. Smaller grid and fewer folds (correct):** 3 x 3 x 3 = 27 combinations times 3 folds = 81 fits, below 100.

## Key idea
Fewer fits come from a smaller grid or fewer folds; parallelism only shortens the time.
Q011510:
## What the tuning model keeps
`CrossValidator.fit` runs 6 x 3 = 18 fits, but the PySpark documentation says `CrossValidatorModel.avgMetrics` holds the average cross-validation metric for each `ParamMap` in `estimatorParamMaps`, in the corresponding order. Since Spark 3.3 `stdMetrics` holds the standard deviation per `ParamMap` as well.
- The list length equals the size of the grid (6), not the number of fits (18) and not the number of folds (3).
- For `rmse`, the best `ParamMap` is the one with the smallest entry; for `r2`, the largest.
- Individual fold models are kept in `subModels` only when `collectSubModels=True` was set before fitting.
- `bestModel` is the refit on the entire dataset, and no metric of that refit is stored in `avgMetrics`.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. One refit metric:** the refit on the full dataset has no held-out data inside the search, so no metric is stored for it.
- ✓ **B. Six averaged values (correct):** each entry is the mean of that combination's three fold metrics, in the same order as the parameter grid.
- ✗ **C. 18 values:** the 18 fold metrics are averaged per combination before they are stored, so the list is not one entry per fit.
- ✗ **D. 3 values:** the average is taken over the folds for each combination, not over the combinations for each fold.

## Key idea
avgMetrics has one entry per ParamMap, averaged over the folds.
Q011511:
## Metrics in the binary evaluator
According to the PySpark documentation, `BinaryClassificationEvaluator` supports exactly two metric names: `areaUnderROC` (the default) and `areaUnderPR`. It reads a `rawPrediction` column (a length-2 vector or a numeric score) and a `label` column.
- `areaUnderROC`: area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (true positive rate against false positive rate across thresholds).
- `areaUnderPR`: area under the precision-recall curve; often more informative when positives are rare.
Metrics such as `f1`, `accuracy` and `logLoss` belong to `MulticlassClassificationEvaluator`. The definitions of the curves are generally accepted.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. areaUnderPR (correct):** this is the documented name for the area under the precision-recall curve in the binary evaluator.
- ✗ **B. prAUC:** this name does not exist in Spark ML; the area metric is named `areaUnderPR`.
- ✗ **C. f1:** valid for the multiclass evaluator, but the binary evaluator rejects it because only the two area metrics are supported.
- ✗ **D. areaUnderRecall:** there is no such metric; recall is a point on a curve and not an area metric in the evaluator.

## Key idea
BinaryClassificationEvaluator = areaUnderROC (default) or areaUnderPR.
Q011512:
## Log loss in Spark ML
Log loss (cross-entropy) averages the negative log of the probability the model assigned to the true class. It punishes confident wrong answers heavily and is lower for better models; this is the generally accepted definition.
- The PySpark docs list `logLoss` among the `MulticlassClassificationEvaluator` metrics (with `f1`, `accuracy`, `hammingLoss`, `weightedPrecision` and others) and state that the `probabilityCol` is only used for `logLoss`.
- Hard class predictions (`prediction`) alone carry no probability, so log loss cannot be computed from them.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Regression mse:** this measures squared distance between class indexes, which have no numeric meaning for classes, and it is not log loss.
- ✗ **B. Binary evaluator:** it supports only `areaUnderROC` and `areaUnderPR`, so `logLoss` is not a valid name.
- ✓ **C. Multiclass evaluator with a probability column (correct):** it is the documented place for `logLoss`, which reads the class probabilities.
- ✗ **D. Only prediction:** the label and hard prediction hold no confidence, and the evaluator needs `probabilityCol` for log loss.

## Key idea
logLoss lives in MulticlassClassificationEvaluator and needs the probability column.
Q011513:
## F1
F1 = 2 x precision x recall / (precision + recall), the harmonic mean (generally accepted definition). Here 2 x 0.90 x 0.30 / 1.20 = 0.45.
- The harmonic mean is pulled toward the smaller value, so a model cannot hide poor recall behind high precision.
- In Spark ML, `MulticlassClassificationEvaluator` uses `f1` as its default metric name (a weighted F1 across classes) and offers `fMeasureByLabel` for one class.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. 0.90:** F1 is limited by the lower of the two values and never follows the higher one.
- ✗ **B. 0.60:** the arithmetic mean is not F1 and hides the weak recall that F1 is meant to expose.
- ✗ **C. 0.27:** the plain product of precision and recall is not scaled by the sum, so it is not F1.
- ✓ **D. 0.45 (correct):** the harmonic mean 2 x 0.90 x 0.30 / (0.90 + 0.30) equals 0.45, well below the mean of the two inputs.

## Key idea
F1 is the harmonic mean of precision and recall, pulled toward the smaller one.
Q011514:
## ROC AUC from hard predictions
The PySpark documentation says the `rawPrediction` column can be a double (a binary 0/1 prediction or the probability of label 1) or a length-2 vector. A 0/1 column is therefore accepted, but it holds only one threshold.
- The ROC curve then has three points: (0, 0), (FPR, TPR) and (1, 1), with FPR = 1 - 0.90 = 0.10 and TPR = 0.80.
- The area under those two line segments is (1 + TPR - FPR) / 2 = (1 + 0.80 - 0.10) / 2 = 0.85, which equals the average of the true positive and true negative rates (balanced accuracy).
- With real scores or probabilities the curve has many points and measures ranking quality, so scores are the better input.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. 0.85 (correct):** a 0/1 column gives a ROC curve with one interior point, and its area is the mean of TPR and TNR, (0.80 + 0.90) / 2.
- ✗ **B. Error:** the documentation lists a double column of 0/1 predictions as valid input, so no error is raised.
- ✗ **C. 0.72:** the product 0.80 x 0.90 is not an area under any ROC curve.
- ✗ **D. 0.90:** the area depends on both rates and is not simply the larger one.

## Key idea
AUC on hard predictions equals balanced accuracy; feed scores to measure ranking.
Q011515:
## Why accuracy is not enough
Accuracy and F1 at a fixed threshold only look at the hard class, so the two models look alike. Log loss (generally accepted definition) uses the probability of the true class, so a prediction of 0.01 for the true class costs far more than one of 0.45.
- Lower log loss is better, so model X (mild errors) beats model Y (confident errors).
- Spark ML computes `logLoss` in `MulticlassClassificationEvaluator`, which needs the probability column.
- `hammingLoss` is the fraction of wrong labels, the same for both models here.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. areaUnderROC:** it measures ranking, never favors "more extreme" mistakes, and there is no reason for it to prefer the confidently wrong model.
- ✗ **B. hammingLoss:** it is the share of wrong labels, which is 10% for both models, so it does not separate them.
- ✓ **C. Log loss (correct):** confident mistakes add a large penalty, so the model with milder errors has the lower loss and wins.
- ✗ **D. F1 at 0.5:** both models make the same number of errors at that threshold, so F1 cannot tell them apart and does not reward confident errors.

## Key idea
Log loss rewards honest uncertainty; threshold metrics ignore it.
Q011516:
## Regression metric names
The PySpark documentation lists the `RegressionEvaluator` metric names:

- `mse`: mean squared error
- `r2`: the R-squared metric
- `mae`: mean absolute error
